citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

The presented normalized Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ has an involutive $A$-linear anti-automorphism $\flat$ defined by $\flat(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}$. It satisfies $\flat(H_w)=H_{w^{-1}}$ for every $w\in S_n$ and commutes with the bar involution: $\flat\circ\iota=\iota\circ\flat$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; every $p_{y,w}$ has integer coefficients and fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

For $n\ge1$, let $r_{y,w}\in A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the $R$-coefficients of [[def-bruhat-interval-and-r-polynomials]]. (a) **Recursion.** Let $w\in S_n$ and let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection with $sw<w$. Then for every $y\in S_n$ $$r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}\quad\text{if }sy<y,\qquad r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}+(v-v^{-1})\,r_{y,sw}\quad\text{if }sy>y .$$ (b) **Support.** $r_{y,w}\ne0$ implies $y\le w$, and $r_{w,w}=1$. (c) **Degree and parity.** For $y\le w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $r_{y,w}\in v^{-d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{2},v^{-2}]$; the term of least $v$-degree is $\mathrm{sgn}(y)\,\mathrm{sgn}(w)\,v^{-d}$, and the term of largest $v$-degree is $v^{d}$. (d) **Symmetry.** $\overline{r_{y,w}}=\mathrm{sgn}(y)\mathrm{sgn}(w)r_{y,w}$ and $r_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=r_{y,w}$. (e) **Matrix inversion.** $\sum_{y\in S_n} r_{x,y}\,\overline{r_{y,z}}=\delta_{x,z}$ for all $x,z$; equivalently the triangular matrices $R=(r_{x,y})$, $\bar R$ satisfy $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$. Here $\mathrm{sgn}(y)=(-1)^{\ell(y)}$ and all coefficients are kept in the variable $v$ of this page.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

derivations.claim: **Well-definedness and bilinearity (1), (2).** Since $\{H_w\}$ is an $A$-basis by [F1], prescribing $\varepsilon(H_w)=\delta_{e,w}$ and extending $A$-linearly is well defined and unique; the reversal map $a$ is a well-defined $A$-linear anti-automorphism by [F2], and multiplication is $A$-bilinear, so $(h,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ is a well-defined $A$-bilinear form, for $(ph,qh')=\varepsilon(p\,a(h)\,q\,h')=pq\,\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ with $p,q\in A$. This proves (1) and (2).

**The key identity: base case and recursion.** We prove by induction on $\ell(u)$ that $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$; for $u=e$ this reads $H_eH_y=H_y$ and $\varepsilon(H_y)=\delta_{e,y}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$, and for $u\ne e$ we choose a simple reflection $s$ with $\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$ and note that [F1] applied to $w=us$ gives $H_{us}H_s=H_u$, since $(us)s=u$ has length $\ell(u)=\ell(us)+1$.

**The left multiplication rule.** Applying the anti-automorphism $a$ of [F2] to the two cases of [F1] and using $a(H_wH_s)=a(H_s)a(H_w)=H_sH_{w^{-1}}$ and $(ws)^{-1}=sw^{-1}$ gives $H_sH_w=H_{sw}$ if $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)+1$, and $H_sH_w=H_{sw}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w$ if $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$; this is the rule used in the two cases below.

**The ascent case.** Keep $u\ne e$ and its right descent $s$ from step 2.1, and let $y\in S_n$ satisfy $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_sH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})$; the induction hypothesis applies to the pair $(us,sy)$, whose first length is $\ell(u)-1$, giving $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,(sy)^{-1}}=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$, and $us=y^{-1}s$ holds if and only if $u=y^{-1}$ (multiply on the right by $s$ and use $s^2=e$), so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$.

**The descent case.** Keep $u,s$ as above and let $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}+(v^{-1}-v)H_y$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})+(v^{-1}-v)\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)$; the induction hypothesis gives $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}}$. If $us=y^{-1}$, then $y=(us)^{-1}=su^{-1}$ and, since $us$ is a right descent of $u$, taking inverses gives $\ell(y)=\ell(su^{-1})=\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$, while $\ell(sy)=\ell(u^{-1})=\ell(u)>\ell(y)$, contradicting $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$; hence $\delta_{us,y^{-1}}=0$ and $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$.

**The induction concludes.** For every $u\ne e$ the cases $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$ and $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$ exhaust all $y$ for the chosen right descent $s$, and each case reduced the first argument's length; with the base case this proves $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$.

**Standard orthonormality (4).** For all $x,y$, using $a(H_x)=H_{x^{-1}}$ from [F2] and step 6.1 with $u=x^{-1}$, we get $(H_x,H_y)=\varepsilon(a(H_x)H_y)=\varepsilon(H_{x^{-1}}H_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y^{-1}}=\delta_{x,y}$, the last equality being injectivity of $w\mapsto w^{-1}$; this proves (4).

**The generator trace identity.** By step 6.1, for every $w$ and simple reflection $s$ one has $\varepsilon(H_wH_s)=\delta_{w,s^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_sH_w)=\delta_{s,w^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$. Extending over the standard basis gives $\varepsilon(zH_s)=\varepsilon(H_sz)$ for every $z\in H$. In particular the common value for $w=s$ is $1$.

**$\varepsilon$ is a trace and yields the adjunctions (3).** Every element of $H$ is a finite $A$-linear combination of words in the generators, and moving each letter of a word for the second factor to the front one at a time with step 7.2 and bilinearity shows $\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(yx)$ for all $x,y\in H$; consequently, for simple $s$ and $h,h'\in H$, using $a(H_s)=H_s$ from [F2], $(hH_s,h')=\varepsilon(a(hH_s)h')=\varepsilon(H_sa(h)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h'H_s)=(h,h'H_s)$ and $(H_sh,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)a(H_s)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)H_sh')=(h,H_sh')$, which proves (3) and shows both left and right multiplication by $H_s$ are self-adjoint for $(-,-)$.

**Values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis (5).** Write $\underline H_x=\sum_{u\le x}h_{u,x}H_u$ with $h_{u,x}=p_{u,x}\in\mathbb Z[v]$, $h_{x,x}=1$ and $h_{u,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $u<x$, all other coefficients zero, as in [F3]; then bilinearity (2) and orthonormality from step 7.1 give $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)=\sum_uh_{u,x}h_{u,y}$. A nonzero term requires $u\le x$ and $u\le y$; if $x
e y$, every surviving term has a factor in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, because $u<x$ or $u<y$ is [F3], and $u=x
e y$ gives $h_{x,y}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ when $x<y$ and $h_{x,y}=0$ otherwise, symmetrically for $u=y$; hence $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $x
e y$. For $x=y$ the term $u=x$ contributes $h_{x,x}^2=1$ and every other term has $u<x$ and contributes to $v^2\mathbb Z[v]$, so $(\underline H_x,\underline H_x)\in 1+v\mathbb Z[v]$.

**The standard pairing (6) and conclusion.** By (4) the form $(-,-)$ is the $A$-bilinear form whose matrix in the normalized standard basis $\{H_x\}$ is the identity; the published type-A Soergel Hom formula uses the standard pairing with $\langle H_x,H_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$ on that normalized basis, and the dictionary of [F4] fixes the normalization $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and the resulting Kazhdan-Lusztig coefficients, so the transported pairing agrees with $(-,-)$ on the basis and hence on $H$ by bilinearity. All six clauses are proved over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using only existence and triangularity of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and no positivity and no choice.

citations.quote: Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. For every $x\in S_n$ there is a unique normalized indecomposable $B_x$ supported on $\{y:y\le x\}$ with top $\Delta$ layer exactly $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. It is the unique summand with the $x$ graph of any reduced Bott-Samelson word for $x$. Every indecomposable is exactly one $B_x(d)$. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, let $B_x$ be the normalized indecomposable bimodule classified by its top support. With right dual $DM=\operatorname{Hom}_{-R}^{\bullet}(M,R)$, one has $DB_x\cong B_x$. Its right reduction has degrees only in $[-\ell(x),\ell(x)]$, all congruent to $\ell(x)$ modulo two, and the two extremal dimensions are one. Hence its reduced graded dimensions are symmetric. Every Bott-Samelson word has a graded perfect symmetric invariant trace form. These assertions assume neither the Kazhdan-Lusztig character conjecture nor hard Lefschetz.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule lying in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that it
carries a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag. Then:

1. the graded multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ of
   [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are
   independent of the compatible enumeration of the flag, so that the character
   sums $h_\Delta(M)$ and $h_\nabla(M)$ are functions of $M$ alone;
2. if $M=M'\oplus M''$ with $M',M''\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, then
   $(M:\Delta_x(d))=(M':\Delta_x(d))+(M'':\Delta_x(d))$ and likewise for
   $\nabla$; more generally the same holds for any direct summand $N$ of $M$
   which itself lies in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that by
[[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] the
multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ and the characters
$h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(M)$ are defined and intrinsic. Then for every simple
reflection $s=s_i$:

1. $B_i\otimes_RM$ and $M\otimes_RB_i$ lie in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, with
   finitely many flag quotients;
2. $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$ and
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$, where
   $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_i+v$ and $\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ is the
   normalized basis of [[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]];
3. for the internal shift and all $k\in\mathbb Z$,
   $h_\Delta(M\{k\})=v^{-k}h_\Delta(M)$ and
   $h_\nabla(M\{k\})=v^{k}h_\nabla(M)$; in the Elias–Williamson notation of the
   sources, whose shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ lowers every generating degree by one,
   this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$ and $h_\nabla$ by
   $v^{-1}$;
4. on $M=R$ the recursion reads $h_\Delta(B_i)=h_\nabla(B_i)=H_i$.

This is a statement about the action of the generators only: multiplicativity of
$h_\Delta$ and $h_\nabla$ for arbitrary tensor products is proved on this page
only after the categorification theorem.

Let $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ be a word in simple reflections and
$B_{\underline i}:=B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$, with
$B_\emptyset=R$. Then $B_{\underline i}$ belongs to both $F_\Delta$ and
$F_\nabla$: it has a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag in the sense of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], its
support is contained in $Gr(S_n)$, and each successive quotient of these flags
is a standard bimodule $R_x\{a\}$ with $x$ a product
$x=s_{i_{j_1}}\cdots s_{i_{j_m}}$ ($1\le j_1<\cdots<j_m\le r$) of a
subexpression of $\underline i$ formed by keeping $m$ letters; the Coxeter
length $\ell(x)$ can be smaller than $m$. The shift $a$ of an occurrence
is computed recursively, one step $\pm1$ per letter of $\underline i$, from the
two rank-one exact sequences of step 1.2 below: the $\Delta$-chart and the
$\nabla$-chart use the two different sequences, so the shift depends on the
chosen subexpression and on the chart, and it is *not* a function of the lengths
and descent numbers of the subexpression alone: for the one-letter word $(s)$
the $\nabla$-chart occurrences are $R\{1\}$ and $R_s\{-1\}$, while the
$\Delta$-chart occurrences are the translates $\Delta_e(1)=R\{-1\}$ and
$\Delta_s(0)=R_s\{1\}$ of the same two subexpressions, so the same subexpression
carries different shifts in the two charts. In particular the number of occurrences of a graph $x$ in the
$\Delta$-flag and in the $\nabla$-flag of $B_{\underline i}$ is the number of
subexpressions of $\underline i$ with product $x$. Moreover $B_{\underline i}$
is finite free of rank $2^r$ as a left
$R$-module and as a right $R$-module, and the flag categories are closed under
tensoring with a generator on either side: if $M\in F_\Delta$ then
$B_s\otimes_RM\in F_\Delta$ and $M\otimes_RB_s\in F_\Delta$, and likewise with
$\nabla$ in place of $\Delta$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection and $w\in S_n$. In the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis $\{\underline H_w\}$ of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]: $$\underline H_s\,\underline H_w=\begin{cases}(v+v^{-1})\,\underline H_w,&sw<w,\\[2pt] \underline H_{sw}+\displaystyle\sum_{\substack{z\in S_n\\ sz<z<w}}\mu(z,w)\,\underline H_z,&sw>w,\end{cases}$$ and symmetrically $\underline H_w\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_w$ if $ws<w$, $\underline H_w\underline H_s=\underline H_{ws}+\sum_{zs<z<w}\mu(z,w)\underline H_z$ if $ws>w$. The span conclusion is for the ascent case $sw>w$: there, $\underline H_s\underline H_w$ lies in the span of $\underline H_{sw}$ and of the $\underline H_z$ with $z<w$ and $sz<z$.

derivations.claim: For finite right-free rational $M,N$, a homogeneous bimodule map is determined by the images of a finite right basis. In a fixed degree the finitely many left-generator commutation relations are finite linear equations with rational coefficients. Their kernel commutes with the flat field extension to $\mathbb R$. Thus every homogeneous Hom space, and its composition, commutes with extension. The support cut on a specified graph union is the common kernel of its finitely generated graph ideal acting on the carrier: the carrier is right-free and generically a sum of reduced graph modules, so the relations hold before localization by torsion-freeness. These kernels commute with flat extension as well. Therefore the canonical support submodules, quotients, graph generator degrees and multiplicities commute with extension. Right reduction commutes with it by tensor associativity and the augmentation map.

Let $A=\operatorname{End}^0(B_x)$ over $\mathbb Q$. By [F1] it is finite-dimensional local with residue $\mathbb Q$, and its maximal ideal $J$ is nilpotent by the finite-algebra proof there. Step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{End}^0(B_x^R)=A\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. The ideal $J\otimes\mathbb R$ is nilpotent and its quotient is $\mathbb R$; an element with nonzero residue is invertible by a finite geometric series after subtracting its scalar part. Hence this algebra is local with residue $\mathbb R$, and $B_x^R$ is indecomposable. Its top support layer is unchanged by step 1.1, so the real classification [F1] identifies it with the same normalized real label. Every real word is the extension of its rational word and its rational finite decomposition; the real classification and uniqueness imply that all real indecomposables and all real decompositions are the corresponding labels and shifts.

Duality exchanges the $\Delta$ and $
abla$ flags: dualize their right-split canonical layer sequences, which reverses order and the homogeneous degrees of their graph generators. A $\Delta_y(d)$ layer dualizes to $
abla_y(-d)$. Therefore normalized self-duality gives $h_\Delta(B_y)=h_
abla(B_y)$ by the weight conventions. The same is true for $B_xB_s$: an invariant isomorphism $B_x	o DB_x$ can be extended by the induced rank-one form construction in [F2], whose mixed-basis matrix has determinant one and yields an invariant isomorphism $B_xB_s	o D(B_xB_s)$. If $S(y)$ holds, both characters of $B_y$ are consequently $\underline H_y$. By [F3],[F4], its endomorphism Hom rank has no negative powers and constant term one. Since the polynomial ring has degree-zero part $\mathbb R$ and no negative degrees, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is then exactly $\mathbb R$.

Step 1.1 proves the support multiplicity, character, Hom and reduction identities in (3). These characters have integer Laurent coefficients recording finite homogeneous graph bases; equality over the real category therefore gives the same integer coefficient equality over the rational category. No injectivity assertion about an unrelated extension of the coefficient ring is needed.

For $xs>x$, assume $S(y)$ for every $y<xs$, including $x$. The tensor $M=B_xB_s$ is a summand of the reduced word for $xs$. Its top layer is the word's unique $\Delta_{xs}$, because the reduced word for $x$ decomposes as $B_x$ and lower-support summands, whose tensor with $B_s$ cannot reach length $\ell(xs)$. By [F1] its unique top summand is therefore $B_{xs}$ unshifted and once; the other summands are $B_y(d)$ with $y<xs$. This top-layer argument makes no substitution of the unknown character of $B_{xs}$.

The character of $M$ is $\underline H_x\underline H_s$, and its standard expansion lies in $\mathbb Z[v]$: the only $v^{-1}$ in simple multiplication multiplies a strictly lower coefficient already divisible by $v$, while the top coefficient is on an ascent. For every lower $y$, the two Hom ranks $\operatorname{Hom}(B_y,M)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(M,B_y)$ are the standard pairings of this polynomial character with $\underline H_y$, using self-duality from step 3.1. Hence they have no negative powers, and both Hom spaces have no negative-degree maps. A summand $B_y(d)$ with $d>0$ gives a negative-degree inclusion from unshifted $B_y$, and one with $d<0$ gives a negative-degree projection to it, by the convention $M(d)_i=M_{i+d}$. Both are impossible. Thus every lower summand is unshifted, proving the ascent statement with its actual nonnegative multiplicities $a_y$. The character of the top summand is not yet required to equal $\underline H_{xs}$, and no equality $a_y=\mu(y,x)$ is inferred.

For $xs<x$ and $S(x)$, the support of $M=B_xB_s$ stays at most $x$: take a reduced word for $x$ ending in $s$; toggling its last letter shows that the graphs $y,ys$ for $y\le x$ stay in this Bruhat interval. Its character is $(v+v^{-1})\underline H_x$ by [F4],[F5], so its top $x$ layer has the two shifts $\Delta_x(1),\Delta_x(-1)$. The maximal-layer splitting proof of [F1] splits off exactly $B_x(1)$ and $B_x(-1)$. Under $S(x)$ their characters already sum to the whole character of $M$. Any remaining nonzero summand would have a nonzero graph layer with a positive integral multiplicity, contradicting its zero character. Thus $M=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$ with no other summands, without assuming $S$ for any other label.

The local algebra and real indecomposability are step 2.1, and the degree-zero scalar assertion under $S(x)$ is step 3.1. Step 2.1 proves classification after extension, step 3.2 proves all base-change identities, and steps 3.3–4.2 prove the two decompositions with their exact stated hypotheses. Normalization and self-duality come from [F2], proved before the character comparisons.

**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

**The bimodule.** Keep the ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$,
the simple reflections $s_i$ and the invariants $R^{s_i}$ of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]], and recall that $R$ is
a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule and that shifts are defined as in
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]. For $1\le i\le n-1$ put
$$B_i:=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1),$$
the balanced tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]])
of the $(R,R^{s_i})$-bimodule $R$ with the $(R^{s_i},R)$-bimodule $R$, equipped
with the total internal grading of the tensor product and then shifted so that
$$(B_i)_d=\bigl(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R\bigr)_{d+1}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z).$$
In the notation of Elias–Williamson the shift $(r)$ has $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$, so
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; in the library convention $M\{r\}_d=M_{d-r}$ this is
$M(1)=M\{-1\}$, i.e. $M(r)=M\{-r\}$ for every integer $r$. Both conventions
appear on this page, and every shifted formula is read through this dictionary;
when no ambiguity is possible we write $M(r)$.

**The two outer actions.** The left $R$-action is $r'(r\otimes r'')=r'r\otimes r''$
and the right $R$-action is $(r\otimes r'')r'=r\otimes r''r'$; both descend to
the balanced tensor product, they commute, they are homogeneous of degree $0$,
and they satisfy $R$-linearity on the relevant side, so $B_i$ is a graded
$(R,R)$-bimodule over $R^{s_i}$-balanced tensors. Explicitly, the $(R,R)$-bimodule
$B_i$ is generated by the two elements $1\otimes1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$, which
are homogeneous of degrees $-1$ and $+1$ respectively: $\alpha_i$ is a
degree-$2$ element of $R$ and the external shift moves degrees by $-1$.

**Elementary structure.** Since $2$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q$, we have the
decomposition $R=R^{s_i}\oplus\alpha_iR^{s_i}$ (the averaging idempotent
$\tfrac12(1+s_i)$ and its complement), so as a graded left $R$-module and again
as a graded right $R$-module
$$B_i\cong R(-1)\oplus R(1),$$
and $B_i$ is finite free of rank two on each side. The Demazure operator
$\partial_i$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]] is
$R^{s_i}$-linear and surjective onto $R^{s_i}$, and
$\partial_i(\alpha_i h)=2h$ for $h\in R^{s_i}$,
a fact used when the exact sequences of $B_i$ are displayed later on this page.

**Small $n$.** For $n=0$ or $n=1$ there are no simple reflections and no
$B_i$. The only word is the empty word, with bimodule $R$; the additive graded
Bott–Samelson category contains all finite direct sums of shifts of $R$ and
all degree-zero bimodule maps between them.

**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

**The reduction.** Work over the ring $S=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of the real
scalar-extension definition ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]),
with $S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$ the ideal of positive-degree elements; the residue
field of the right action is
$$k:=S/S_+=\mathbb R,$$
with quotient map $S\twoheadrightarrow k$, $s\mapsto \bar s$. For a graded
$(S,S)$-bimodule $M$ that is finite free as a right $S$-module put
$$\overline M:=M\otimes_Sk=M/MS_+,$$
the **reduction** of $M$: a finite-dimensional graded $k$-vector space, on which
the left $S$-action descends because $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $MS_+$ is
stable under left multiplication. Write $\overline M^{\,i}$ for its homogeneous
component of degree $i$, $d_i(M):=\dim_{\mathbb R}\overline M^{\,i}$ for the
graded dimensions, and
$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Indeed, $(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)=c_{w^{-1}(i)}-c_{w^{-1}(i+1)}$ is positive
exactly when $w^{-1}(i)<w^{-1}(i+1)$, the left-ascent criterion for inversion
length. Thus the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The reduced module $\overline{B_x^R}$ has bottom degree
$-\ell(x)$ and top degree $+\ell(x)$; the unreduced bimodule has nonzero
components in arbitrarily high degrees. On a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].

**The setting.** Keep $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$, the
place-permutation action of $S_n$, the balanced roots
$\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$ with $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$ and the
graded $(R,R)$-bimodules $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]; recall that
$1\otimes1\in B_i$ has degree $-1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$ has degree $1$, that
$B_i$ is generated as an $(R,R)$-bimodule by $1\otimes1$, and that $R=R^{s_i}\oplus\alpha_iR^{s_i}$ with
$s_i(\alpha_i)=-\alpha_i$
([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]],
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]).

**The positive generator complex.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ let $F_i$ be the
bounded cochain complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$F_i:=\bigl[\;B_i\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon_i\ }R(1)\;\bigr],$$
with $B_i$ in cohomological degree $0$, $R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and
all other terms zero, where $\varepsilon_i:B_i\to R(1)$ is the
multiplication map $\varepsilon_i(r\otimes r')=rr'$, i.e. the degree-zero
bimodule map determined by $\varepsilon_i(1\otimes1)=1$ and
$\varepsilon_i(1\otimes\alpha_i)=\alpha_i$.

**The negative generator complex.** Let $F_i^{-1}$ be the bounded cochain
complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$F_i^{-1}:=\bigl[\;R(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \eta_i\ }B_i\;\bigr],$$
with $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$, $B_i$ in cohomological degree $0$ and
all other terms zero, where $\eta_i:R(-1)\to B_i$ is the bimodule map
$\eta_i(1)=\alpha_i\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_i$.

**Well-definedness of the differentials.** The map $\varepsilon_i$ descends
from the multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbb Q}R\to R$ because
$\varepsilon_i(ra\otimes r')=rar'=\varepsilon_i(r\otimes ar')$ for $a\in R^{s_i}$
and $R$ is commutative; it is left and right $R$-linear and homogeneous of
degree zero, since $1\otimes1\mapsto1$ matches the degrees $-1$ of $B_i$ and of
the generator of $R(1)$, and $1\otimes\alpha_i\mapsto\alpha_i$ matches the
degree $1=\deg(\alpha_i)-1$ on both sides. For $\eta_i$, the bimodule map
$R\to B_i$ sending $1$ to the class of $x_i-x'_{i+1}$ is well defined: the
products $(x_i-x'_{i+1})(x_i-x'_i)$ and
$(x_i-x'_{i+1})(x_{i+1}-x'_{i+1})$ vanish in $B_i$ by the explicit computation
of GKS Lemma 3.8, while for $a\notin\{i,i+1\}$ the factor $x_a-x'_a$ is already
a defining relation of $B_i$, so the element annihilates the kernel ideal of the
multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbb Q}R\to R$, and the assignment $1\mapsto x_i-x'_{i+1}$
extends to a well-defined $R$-bimodule map. The value of that map at $1$ times
the unit $2\varepsilon_i$ is $\eta_i(1)$, because
$$1\otimes(x_i-x_{i+1})+(x_i-x_{i+1})\otimes1=2(x_i-x'_{i+1})$$
in $B_i$ (GKS Lemma 3.8, using $x_i+x_{i+1}=x'_i+x'_{i+1}$) and
$\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$; a unit multiple of a well-defined
bimodule map is a well-defined bimodule map, so $\eta_i$ is well defined. Its
value $\eta_i(1)$ is homogeneous of degree $1$, matching the degree of
$1\in R(-1)$, so $\eta_i$ is a degree-zero bimodule map. Both complexes are
concentrated in two adjacent cohomological
degrees, so $d^2=0$ holds trivially and each of $F_i,F_i^{-1}$ is a bounded
cochain complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules in the sense of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]].

**Size and consequences.** The bimodules $R$, $R(1)$ and $R(-1)$ are free of
rank one on both sides and $B_i$ is free of rank two on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]], the bases
being $\{1\otimes1,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ on the left and
$\{1\otimes1,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ on the right). Every term of $F_i$ and of
$F_i^{-1}$ is therefore finite free, hence finite graded projective, as a left
$R$-module and as an underlying right $R$-module. Applying
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]]
with the commutative ring $\mathbb Q$ and $A=B=R$: the signed totalization with
$F_i$ is an exact triangulated functor on bounded complexes of finite graded
projective $R$-modules, preserves quasi-isomorphisms between bounded complexes,
and descends to the derived tensor functor $F_i\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}-$ on
$D^b(R\text{-grmod})$; the same statements hold with $F_i^{-1}$ in place of
$F_i$. The right-tensor construction $-\otimes_RF_i$ is defined separately by
signed totalization, and its derived version uses the same two-sided
freeness. Commutativity of $R$ does not assert a symmetry between tensor
products of arbitrary $(R,R)$-bimodules.

**Recorded convention.** The complex $F_i$ is the library normalization of
Rouquier's positive complex $F_s=[A\otimes_{A^s}A\to A]$, in which $A$ sits in
degree $1$ and the differential is multiplication: in the library external
shift $(r)$ with $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$ one has $F_i=T_i(1)$ and
$F_i^{-1}\cong T_i^{-1}(-1)$ for the GKS complexes
$T_i=[B_i(-1)\to R]$, $T_i^{-1}=[R\to B_i(1)]$ of formula (3.3). The GKS negative differential sends $1$ to
$x_i-x'_{i+1}$, whereas ours is $2\varepsilon_i$ times that map.
The chain isomorphism $F_i^{-1}\to T_i^{-1}(-1)$ is multiplication by
$2\varepsilon_i$ in degree $-1$ and the identity in degree $0$.
The internal shifts cancel in inverse pairs and agree on the two sides of
each positive braid relation. The sign $\varepsilon_i$
in $\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$, and with it the sign of $\eta_i$, is
a unit of $\mathbb Q$; the homotopy classes of the complexes do not depend on
the choice of balanced root.

**The construction.** For a signed word
$$\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},\qquad \epsilon_k\in\{\pm1\},\ 1\le i_k\le n-1,$$
put
$$F(\sigma):=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},$$
the iterated signed tensor totalization of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]] of
the Rouquier generator complexes of
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], bracketed left to
right; the empty word ($r=0$) is sent to the unit complex $R$ concentrated in
cohomological degree $0$. This is the **Rouquier complex of the word**. When
$\epsilon_k=+1$ the letter contributes the positive complex $F_{i_k}$ and when
$\epsilon_k=-1$ it contributes $F_{i_k}^{-1}$.

**Structure.** $F(\sigma)$ is a bounded cochain complex of graded
$(R,R)$-bimodules with degree-zero differentials, concentrated in cohomological
degrees $-r_-,\ldots,r_+$, where $r_-$ and $r_+$ count the negative and
positive letters: the term $F(\sigma)^m$ is the direct sum of the
$\binom{r}{m+r_-}$ tensor products of one term of each factor, since the
minimal choice has degree $-r_-$ and each upper-term choice adds one. It carries a
cohomological degree and an internal grading, and the differential is the
Koszul totalization differential. A positive letter contributes its unit term
$R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and the internal shift $(1)$ to that term; a
negative letter contributes its unit term $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$
and the internal shift $(-1)$. Every term is a finite direct sum of finite tensor products of copies
of $R(\pm1)$ and $B_i$, hence is finite free on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]), so each term
is finite graded projective as a left module and as a right module and $F(\sigma)$ defines a
derived tensor functor by
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]].

**Status of the notation.** The notation records the chosen word $(\sigma)$
together with the chosen bracket; it asserts nothing about independence of the
word, of the sign normalization or of the bracketing. That the homotopy class
of $F(\sigma)$ depends only on the braid represented by $\sigma$ is the content
of [[thm-rouquier-complex-is-well-defined-up-to-canonical-homotopy-equivalence]],
whose proof uses the braid relations of the generator complexes and could not be
stated before those relations were proved.

**Convention for comparison.** The library's positive generator $F_i$ is
Rouquier's $F_{s_i}=[A\otimes_{A^{s_i}}A\to A]$ with the library external shift
$(1)$ on both terms, after giving the polynomial variables degree $2$:
$$F_i=[(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R)(1)\longrightarrow R(1)].$$
Rouquier's negative complex of §3.2.4 becomes $F_i^{-1}$ after doubling
internal degrees and shifting the whole complex by $(-1)$, up to the unit
scalar coming from the root normalization. As recorded in
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], the
complexes of Rouquier, Gorsky–Kivinen–Simental, Khovanov and Elias–Krasner
differ from $F_i$ and $F_i^{-1}$ by homological or internal shifts, so any
comparison with those sources is read through the dictionary recorded there.
The empty word corresponds to the trivial braid and to the identity functor.

derivations.claim: **The single-factor identity.** Let $s$ be a simple reflection with root $\alpha=\alpha_s$, let $\mathrm{Br}(b):=bc_s$ on $B_s$, and let $\sigma\in S$. For every $b\in B_s$ one has $\sigma\cdot b=b\cdot(s\sigma)+\partial_s(\sigma)\,\mathrm{Br}(b)$. Indeed both sides are right $S$-linear in $b$, so it suffices to check the two basis elements: for $b=c_{\mathrm{id}}$ the identity is the rule $r\cdot c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot sr+\partial_s(r)c_s$ of [F1] with $r=\sigma$, and for $b=c_s$ it reads $\sigma\cdot c_s=c_s\cdot s\sigma+\partial_s(\sigma)c_s\alpha_s$, which is $c_s\sigma=c_s(s\sigma+\alpha_s\partial_s(\sigma))$ and holds because $\sigma-s\sigma=\alpha_s\partial_s(\sigma)$ and $c_s$ commutes with $S$.

**Iteration over the letters proves (a).** For $m=0$ both outer actions are multiplication by $\rho$ on $S$. For $m>0$, put $\sigma_0=\rho$ and $\sigma_i=s_i\sigma_{i-1}$. Apply step 1.1 in slot $i$ to the remainder $b_1\cdots b_{i-1}(\sigma_{i-1}b_i)b_{i+1}\cdots b_m$. This produces $\partial_{s_i}(\sigma_{i-1})\mathrm{Br}_i(b)$ and a remainder with $\sigma_i$ acting on the right of slot $i$. Balancing moves that polynomial to the left of slot $i+1$; at the last slot it is the outer right action by $x^{-1}\rho$. Each $\sigma_{i-1}$ is linear, so $\partial_{s_i}(\sigma_{i-1})=\sigma_{i-1}(\alpha_{s_i}^\vee)=\gamma_i$. Also $bc_s=\mu(b)c_s$ in one factor: on $c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $c_s$ this follows from $\mu(c_{\mathrm{id}})=1$, $\mu(c_s)=\alpha_s$ and $c_s^2=c_s\alpha_s$. Thus $\mathrm{Br}_i=\chi_i\varphi_i$ with the appropriate shift of $\chi_i$, and the stated degree-two identity holds on every tensor monomial and hence on the whole bimodule.

**The covariance identity.** For all $b,b'\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ and all $i$ one has $\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_i b'\rangle=\langle\varphi_ib,\varphi_ib'\rangle_i$. It suffices to check on tensor monomials $b=b_1\cdots b_m$, $b'=b'_1\cdots b'_m$: the left side is $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((b_1b'_1)\cdots(b_ib'_ic_{s_i})\cdots(b_mb'_m)\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)c_{s_i}\cdots(b_mb'_m)\bigr)$, using $b_ic_{s_i}=\mu(b_i)c_{s_i}$ from step 2.1, so this equals $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\chi_i((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)\cdots(b_mb'_m))\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_i((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)\cdots(b_mb'_m))=\langle\varphi_ib,\varphi_ib'\rangle_i$, using $\operatorname{Tr}\circ\chi_i=\operatorname{Tr}_i$ and the multiplicativity of the ring structure.

**The rescaled form identity (b).** With $\varphi=\sum_i\varphi_i$ and $\langle-,-\rangle'=\bigoplus_i\langle-,-\rangle_i'$, the direct sum decomposition is orthogonal, so for all $b,b'$ one has $\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle'=\sum_i\gamma_i\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle$; substituting step 3.1 gives $\sum_i\gamma_i\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle=\langle b,\sum_i\gamma_i\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle$, and substituting the factorization of step 2.1 gives $\langle b,\rho b'\rangle-\langle b,b'\cdot x^{-1}\rho\rangle$. The second summand is $-\langle b,b'\rangle\,x^{-1}\rho$ by right $S$-linearity of the form, and it vanishes after reduction because $x^{-1}\rho$ has positive degree; hence $\langle b,\rho b'\rangle_{\overline{\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)}}=\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle'$ for $b,b'$ in the reduced module, as claimed in (b).

**Positivity for reduced words and the vanished remainder (c).** Let $\underline x$ be reduced. For each $i$, the prefix $w_i:=s_{i-1}\cdots s_1$ has length $i-1$ and $s_iw_i$ has length $i$; the descent criterion [F3] therefore gives $\gamma_i=(w_i\rho)(\alpha_{s_i}^\vee)>0$. All rescalings are by strictly positive real numbers, so no sign in a definite form changes; and the polynomial $x^{-1}\rho$ lies in $S_2\subset S_+$ whose right multiplication lands in $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)S_+$, which becomes zero after reduction, so the remainder vanishes on the reduced module. This proves (c).

**Identification with the Rouquier differential (d).** By [F4] the first differential of the Rouquier complex is the sum, over the letters, of the maps $\varphi_i$ from the cohomological degree $0$ term $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ to the degree $1$ term $\bigoplus_i\mathrm{BS}(\widehat{\underline x}_i)(1)$, and its dual maps decompose the generator $c_{s_i}$ back, i.e. are the maps $\chi_i$ with the displayed internal shifts. Composing the differential with the rescaled dual maps $\gamma_i\chi_i$ and summing over $i$ gives $\sum_i\gamma_i\mathrm{Br}_i$, which by step 2.1 equals left multiplication by $\rho$ modulo the right-multiplication remainder that vanishes on the reduced module by step 5.1. Hence left multiplication by $\rho$ on the reduced Bott-Samelson module factors, up to the positive rescalings $\gamma_i$, as the composite $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bigoplus_i\mathrm{BS}(\widehat{\underline x}_i)(1)\xrightarrow{\ \gamma\chi\ }\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(2)$ built from the first Rouquier differential and its dual; all first-differential Koszul signs are $+1$, because every preceding tensor factor is in cohomological degree zero, so this is exactly $\rho\cdot(-)$ after right reduction. This proves (d) and completes the lemma; no positivity of characters and no character conjecture is used.

**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=\underline H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form when $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here $d=\ell(x)$ by the proved normalized degree bounds. The property $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ always denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on $\overline{B_x^R}$, independently of $\mathrm{S}(x)$. $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the conjunction of $\mathrm{S}(x)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations with the standard sign for this normalized intrinsic form; its existence and uniqueness, and the nonzero positive bottom value used for normalization, are proved in [[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires the general Hodge-Riemann relations above for the restricted intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional over a field of characteristic not $2$. Every symmetric bilinear form $B$ on $V$ admits a basis whose distinct vectors are pairwise orthogonal for $B$.

Every symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space is congruent to exactly one normal form

$$\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q,0_r),\qquad p+q+r=\dim V.$$

Equivalently, the numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries are independent of the diagonalizing basis.

Let $B$ be a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space, and write $q(v):=B(v,v)$. The form is **positive definite** when $q(v)>0$ for every $v\ne0$, and **negative definite** when $q(v)<0$ for every $v\ne0$. The same terminology applies to the associated quadratic form.

Suppose a basis gives a diagonal matrix with $p$ positive diagonal entries, $q$ negative diagonal entries, and $r$ zero entries. Its **inertia** is the triple $(p,q,r)$, its **rank** is $p+q$, and its **signature** is $p-q$. Sylvester's law of inertia proves that this triple is independent of the diagonalizing basis, and therefore justifies the notation.

Let $B$ be a bilinear form on an $n$-dimensional vector space $V$, and let $\mathcal B=(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis. The **matrix of $B$ in $\mathcal B$** is

$$[B]_{\mathcal B}:=(B(v_i,v_j))_{i,j<n}.$$

For coordinate columns $x=[u]_{\mathcal B}$ and $y=[v]_{\mathcal B}$, one has $B(u,v)=x^{\mathsf T}[B]_{\mathcal B}y$.

The **left radical** and **right radical** are

$$\operatorname{rad}_L(B):=\{u:B(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\},\qquad \operatorname{rad}_R(B):=\{v:B(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}.$$

The **rank of $B$** is the rank of the associated map $B^\flat:V\to V^*$, $B^\flat(u)(v)=B(u,v)$. The form is **nondegenerate** when both radicals are zero. In finite dimension this is equivalent to $B^\flat$ being an isomorphism, and also to $[B]_{\mathcal B}$ being invertible.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=\underline H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form when $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here $d=\ell(x)$ by the proved normalized degree bounds. The property $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ always denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on $\overline{B_x^R}$, independently of $\mathrm{S}(x)$. $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the conjunction of $\mathrm{S}(x)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations with the standard sign for this normalized intrinsic form; its existence and uniqueness, and the nonzero positive bottom value used for normalization, are proved in [[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires the general Hodge-Riemann relations above for the restricted intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.

derivations.claim: **One step of the decomposition.** Under hL the map $L^{i+2}:H^{-i-2}\to H^{i+2}$ is an isomorphism, so for every $a\in H^{-i}$ there is $b\in H^{-i-2}$ with $L^{i+1}a=L^{i+2}b$; then $a-Lb\in P_L^{-i}$, and hence $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}+L\,H^{-i-2}$. The sum is direct: if $Lb\in P_L^{-i}$, then $0=L^{i+1}(Lb)=L^{i+2}b$ and injectivity of $L^{i+2}$ gives $b=0$; hence $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}\oplus L\,H^{-i-2}$.

**Iteration and the primitive decomposition (a).** Iterating step 1.1 gives $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}\oplus L\,P_L^{-i-2}\oplus L^2P_L^{-i-4}\oplus\cdots=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^kP_L^{-(i+2k)}$, the sum terminating because $H^{-m}=0$ for $m>d$; For positive degree $i$, hL gives $H^i=L^iH^{-i}$, so applying $L^i$ to the negative-degree decomposition supplies all positive pieces. Reindexing by the lowest primitive degree gives $H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$, since every string $L^kP_L^{-i}$ lies in degrees between $-i$ and $i$, so $k\le i$ for nonzero contributions. This proves (a).

**Orthogonality (b).** Let $p\in P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ and $q\in P_L^{-(i+2l)}$ with $k<l$ and consider $a=L^kp$, $b=L^lq$ in $H^{-i}$. Using symmetry of $L$ repeatedly, $(a,b)_L^{-i}=\langle L^kp,L^{i+l}q\rangle=\langle p,L^{i+k+l}q\rangle$, and the exponent satisfies $i+k+l\ge i+2k+1$; since $L^{i+2k+1}p=0$, the pairing vanishes. Hence distinct strings are orthogonal for the Lefschetz form, as claimed.

**Non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms is equivalent to hL (c).** For fixed $i$, the Lefschetz form at degree $-i$ is the composite of the linear map $L^i:H^{-i}\to H^i$ with the perfect pairing $H^i\times H^{-i}\to\mathbb R$ given by the form; the latter is an isomorphism $H^i\to(H^{-i})^*$ by non-degeneracy of $\langle-,-\rangle$ [F1]. Hence the Lefschetz form is non-degenerate if and only if $L^i$ is an isomorphism; this holds simultaneously for all $i\ge0$ exactly when hL holds, and for $i>d$ both sides are zero by [F1] ($\dim H^i=\dim H^{-i}=0$). This proves (c).

**Signature formula (d).** Assume hL and the standard-sign definiteness on primitives. The orthogonal decomposition of step 3.1 expresses the form on $H^{-i}$ as an orthogonal sum of the forms $(p,q)\mapsto\langle p,L^{i+2k}q\rangle$ on the primitive spaces $P_L^{-(i+2k)}$; each of these is definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i-2k)/2}$ by HR, and its own inertia is therefore $(\dim P,0,0)$ or $(0,\dim P,0)$ according to that sign. Sylvester's law [F2] makes the signature of the orthogonal sum the sum of the summand signatures, giving the displayed formula. Conversely, assume hL and the signature formula for all $i$; descending from the bottom degree, the formula determines the signature of the primitive form on $P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ after the signatures of the higher-degree primitive spaces are known, the orthogonal decomposition and step 4.1 make each primitive form non-degenerate, and the subtraction forces its signature to be the prescribed sign times its dimension. Its inertia therefore has only positive or only negative entries by [F2], so each primitive form is definite with the stated sign; this recovers HR. This proves (d).

**Stable subspaces (e).** Let $V\subseteq H$ be $L$-stable with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$. Since $L^i$ is injective on $H$ (hL), its restriction to $V$ is injective, and the dimension symmetry makes it an isomorphism onto $V^i$; hence $V$ satisfies hL for the restricted operator and form. Its primitive spaces are $P_V^{-i}=V^{-i}\cap P_L^{-i}$, because the kernel of $L^{i+1}$ on $V^{-i}$ is the intersection with the kernel on $H^{-i}$; the restricted Lefschetz form on $P_V^{-i}$ is the restriction of the ambient definite primitive form, hence definite with the ambient sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$. The string construction in steps 1.1–2.1 uses only hL, so it applies to $V$ before non-degeneracy of its restricted form is known. This primitive decomposition then shows, exactly as in step 5.1, that the restricted form on $V$ is an orthogonal sum of definite blocks, hence non-degenerate, and that its signs are the ambient signs; if the lowest nonzero degree of $V$ equals $-d$, then the ambient sign formula is also the standard sign of $V$. This proves (e) and completes the lemma.

boundaries.evidence: For the zero space every summand in the decompositions of step 2.1 and step 4.1 is zero and the assertions hold vacuously; the string sum of step 2.1 is finite and terminates once the degree leaves the range of H.

Zero operators and zero pairings are covered: step 1.1 subtracts Lb, which may already be zero, to reach a primitive vector, and the strings L^k P^{-(i+2k)} are zero once the degree drops below the lowest degree, which is why step 2.1 terminates.
A length-one string is the k = 0 term of the decomposition in step 2.1, and the direct summand P_L^{-i} constructed in step 1.1 is exactly the primitive part of the degree -i piece.
Statement (e) explicitly assumes ambient hL; without it L=0 on nonzero degrees ±1 would violate the original inheritance claim. Lefschetz-form degeneracy is characterized by (c).

Both grading ends are used: the decomposition of step 2.1 terminates at the top degree, and the signature formula proved in step 5.1 is anchored at the lowest nonzero degree where the primitive form is the whole space.
Choice-free: the decompositions are taken in finite-dimensional real vector spaces and the complements are built from finitely many vectors in step 1.1, so no infinite selection is required.

Forward direction of the exactly-when clause: step 4.1 writes the Lefschetz form at degree -i as the composite of L^i with a perfect pairing, so non-degeneracy forces L^i injective, and the dimension symmetry recorded there upgrades this to an isomorphism, which is hL.

Reverse direction: if L^i is an isomorphism then the composite form of step 4.1 is a perfect pairing, so every Lefschetz form is non-degenerate; step 3.1 supplies the orthogonal decomposition used to recognize the non-degenerate direct sum.

Reviewed all six steps and the current primitive, inertia, orthogonal-basis and rank-nullity interfaces. The hL string splitting terminates, positive pieces follow by L^i, string orthogonality transfers powers to the shorter primitive string, and perfect graded pairing gives both directions of nondegenerate Lefschetz forms iff hL.
