Let $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ be a word in simple reflections and
$B_{\underline i}:=B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$, with
$B_\emptyset=R$. Then $B_{\underline i}$ belongs to both $F_\Delta$ and
$F_\nabla$: it has a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag in the sense of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], its
support is contained in $Gr(S_n)$, and each successive quotient of these flags
is a standard bimodule $R_x\{a\}$ with $x$ a product
$x=s_{i_{j_1}}\cdots s_{i_{j_m}}$ ($1\le j_1<\cdots<j_m\le r$) of a
subexpression of $\underline i$ formed by keeping $m$ letters; the Coxeter
length $\ell(x)$ can be smaller than $m$. The shift $a$ of an occurrence
is computed recursively, one step $\pm1$ per letter of $\underline i$, from the
two rank-one exact sequences of step 1.2 below: the $\Delta$-chart and the
$\nabla$-chart use the two different sequences, so the shift depends on the
chosen subexpression and on the chart, and it is *not* a function of the lengths
and descent numbers of the subexpression alone: for the one-letter word $(s)$
the $\nabla$-chart occurrences are $R\{1\}$ and $R_s\{-1\}$, while the
$\Delta$-chart occurrences are the translates $\Delta_e(1)=R\{-1\}$ and
$\Delta_s(0)=R_s\{1\}$ of the same two subexpressions, so the same subexpression
carries different shifts in the two charts. In particular the number of occurrences of a graph $x$ in the
$\Delta$-flag and in the $\nabla$-flag of $B_{\underline i}$ is the number of
subexpressions of $\underline i$ with product $x$. Moreover $B_{\underline i}$
is finite free of rank $2^r$ as a left
$R$-module and as a right $R$-module, and the flag categories are closed under
tensoring with a generator on either side: if $M\in F_\Delta$ then
$B_s\otimes_RM\in F_\Delta$ and $M\otimes_RB_s\in F_\Delta$, and likewise with
$\nabla$ in place of $\Delta$.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule lying in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that it
carries a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag. Then:

1. the graded multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ of
   [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are
   independent of the compatible enumeration of the flag, so that the character
   sums $h_\Delta(M)$ and $h_\nabla(M)$ are functions of $M$ alone;
2. if $M=M'\oplus M''$ with $M',M''\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, then

   $\nabla$; more generally the same holds for any direct summand $N$ of $M$
   which itself lies in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$.

Let $x\ne y\in S_n$ and let $r:=n-\dim V^{x^{-1}y}$ be the codimension in
either graph of the intersection $Gr(x)\cap Gr(y)$; here $x^{-1}y$ acts on
$V=k^n$ by place permutation, so $r=1$ exactly when $x^{-1}y$ is a reflection.

1. If $r\ge2$, then every graded short exact sequence of graded $R$-bimodules

2. If $y=xt$ for a reflection $t$, then $r=1$ and every such extension splits

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis

(1) The quotient $\mathcal B^{ss}$ is semisimple with simple classes $B_x(k)$ and endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$, and $q$ reflects isomorphisms.

(2) Every bounded complex of $\mathcal B$ has a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, and any two minimal models are isomorphic as complexes.

(3) Every direct summand of a perverse (respectively p-split) bimodule is perverse (respectively p-split).

(4) For perverse $M,N$ one has $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N(-i))=0$ for $i>0$.

(5) The perverse cuts on p-split bimodules are independent of the chosen decomposition and are preserved by every morphism.

derivations.claim: Induct on the word length. For the empty word $F_e=R$ has just $\Delta_e$; for one letter the exact rank-one sequence is $0\to R_s(-1)\to B_s\xrightarrow{\mu}R(1)\to0$. Its upper $s$ layer is $R_s(-1)=\Delta_s$, and its identity layer is the isomorphism $R(1)\to R(1)$, hence contractible. This starts the induction directly for positive complexes; no inverse generator is identified with a positive one.

Choose a Bruhat-compatible enumeration grouped into right-$s$ cosets, listing $y$ before $ys$ when $y<ys$. This exists by ordering the minimal representatives of the finite cosets in Bruhat order and refining each pair; the lifting property from reduced subwords ensures that different coset comparisons respect this order. Every union of complete initial or terminal cosets is right-$s$-stable. For such a set $A$, $\Gamma_A(MB_s)=\Gamma_A(M)B_s$: the cut and quotient have graph flags, whose free layers split on the right; after exact tensoring, their generic graph supports lie respectively in $A$ and its stable complement. The quotient remains right-free by its flag, so an $A$-supported element of it is generically zero and hence zero. This proves the cut identity and its analogous consecutive-coset quotient identity.

Write $x=zs$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(z)+1$. Every term of $F_z$ is supported on subexpressions of a reduced word for $z$, hence on labels at most $z$. In particular its $x$ layer is zero termwise, not merely contractible. Its paired layer on $\{z,x\}$ is therefore its single $z$ layer, homotopy equivalent as a full bimodule complex to $\Delta_z$ by induction. The cut identity of step 1.2 identifies the paired layer of $F_zF_s$ with the cone of the natural multiplication map from this paired layer tensored with $B_s$ to its shift $(1)$. A full bimodule homotopy equivalence commutes with this natural counit and induces a homotopy equivalence of the cones. Thus this paired layer is the rank-one graph complex $[R_z(-\ell(z))B_s\to R_z(-\ell(z)+1)]$. Its high $x$ layer is the kernel graph $R_x(-\ell(x))=\Delta_x$, and its low $z$ layer is an isomorphism onto $R_z(-\ell(z)+1)$ and contracts. The two single-layer functors of the paired layer are the original canonical single layers: the support cut and quotient flag, in the chosen enumeration, contain exactly those two labels, so their submodule and quotient are respectively its high and low graph layers. This proves the two required layers with the counit compatibility retained.

On any other pair, both single layers of $F_z$ contract by induction. Their paired sequence becomes termwise split after restriction to right $R^s$, by [F1]. Tensoring with $B_s$ yields a triangle with contractible outside terms, so its paired tensor layer contracts. Applying either single-layer functor preserves its homotopy and gives contractible single layers of $F_zB_s$. The same single layers of $F_z(1)$ contract already by induction. Since $F_zF_s$ is the cone of the natural multiplication map $F_zB_s\to F_z(1)$ with its standard shift, and an additive layer functor commutes with cones, both resulting single layers also contract. This treats every non-top pair without claiming that arbitrary complexes with zero Euler character contract.

The paired enumeration covers every graph; its single layers equal the canonical Bruhat layers by [F1]. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the asserted homotopy isomorphism for the word complex. By [F3] every layer of a removed contractible summand remains contractible, so the same isomorphism holds for its minimal summand. This is exactly the stated $\Delta$-split property, obtained without any $S$ or Hodge assumption.

**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

**The operator.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$, a strictly dominant
$\rho\in S_2$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]])
and a real parameter $\zeta\ge0$. On the tensor product
$B_x^RB_s^R=B_x^R\otimes_SB_s^R$ define
$$L_\zeta:=(\rho\cdot(-))\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B_s^R}+\mathrm{id}_{B_x^R}\otimes(\zeta\,\rho\cdot(-)),$$
where the first summand is left multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor and
the second summand is left multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the second factor.
Because the polynomial ring is commutative and the balanced tensor product
identifies $b r\otimes c=b\otimes rc$ for $r\in S$, the second summand equals
right multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the first factor; both summands are
degree-two, $S$-linear on the right, and commute, so $L_\zeta$ is a degree-two
right-$S$-linear endomorphism of $B_x^RB_s^R$. In particular $L_\zeta$ preserves
the submodule $MS_+$ for $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$\mathbb R$-linear endomorphism of the reduced module
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ ([[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]
supplies the induced invariant form and the reduction conventions of
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]] apply).

**Symmetry.** Each summand of $L_\zeta$ is multiplication by an element in the
commutative position algebra of the tensor product: the first is multiplication
by $\rho$ on the first factor, the second is right (equivalently middle)
multiplication by $\zeta\rho$, which is self-adjoint for the induced invariant
form by the invariance identities of the form. Hence $L_\zeta$ is symmetric for
the induced form, and the Lefschetz forms $(\ ,\ )^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ and the
primitive subspaces $P^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ are those of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]] for this
operator.

**The deformation statements.** Write $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$,
$\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ for centered hard
Lefschetz, the Hodge-Riemann relations and the strong embedded-form statement on
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ for the operator $L_\zeta$, with the bottom degree
$-\ell(x)-1$ and the standard sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ of the dictionary in
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]; the
definitions of $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form respectively to all choices of such forms.
At $\zeta=0$ the operator $L_0=\rho\cdot(-)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is left
multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor, so the zero-parameter statements
$\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ are exactly
the undeformed statements $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$,
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ of the dictionary. For fixed data the family
$\zeta\mapsto L_\zeta$ is polynomial of degree one in $\zeta$.

**Summand stability.** Any direct summand $B\subseteq B_x^RB_s^R$ that is a
sub-bimodule is stable under $L_0$, because left multiplication by the central
element $\rho$ is a bimodule endomorphism; stability under $L_\zeta$ for
$\zeta>0$ is a separate condition, since a projector onto $B$ need not commute
with the middle-position operator. The undeformed summand implications used in
the induction of this page are supplied by the local restriction lemma later on
this page, after deforming the parameter back to $\zeta=0$; no statement of this
definition identifies a restricted positive-parameter operator with a
restriction of $L_\zeta$.

**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

Let $H$ have a graded non-degenerate symmetric form and a symmetric degree-two operator $L$.

(a) If hL holds then $H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$; more precisely, in each degree $-i$ one has $H^{-i}=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^kP_L^{-(i+2k)}$.

(b) In each degree $-i$, the decomposition of (a) is orthogonal for the Lefschetz form $\langle a,L^ib\rangle$.

(c) All Lefschetz forms on $H^{-i}$ are non-degenerate exactly when hL holds.

(d) If $H$ has one parity and lowest degree $-d$, standard HR is equivalent to hL together with the signature formula $\operatorname{sig}\bigl(\langle-,L^i-\rangle|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^{(d-i-2k)/2}\dim P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ for every $i\ge0$ (zero spaces omitted).

(e) If $H$ satisfies hL, an $L$-stable graded subspace $V\subseteq H$ with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$ inherits hL; if $H$ satisfies HR then the restricted form on $V$ is non-degenerate and $V$ inherits the ambient primitive signs, and its standard global sign agrees with that of $H$ when their lowest degrees coincide.

(1) **Family lemma.** Let $L_t$, $t\in[a,b]$, be a continuous family of symmetric degree-two operators on $H$, each satisfying hL, and suppose $L_{t_0}$ satisfies HR with the standard sign for one $t_0\in[a,b]$. Then every $L_t$ satisfies HR with the standard sign; in the application the family is $L_\zeta$, $\zeta\ge0$, which is polynomial (hence continuous) in $\zeta$.

(2) **Weak-Lefschetz substitute.** Let $\varphi:V\to W(1)$ be a map of graded $R[L]$-modules such that (a) $\varphi$ is injective in degrees $\le-1$, (b) $V,W$ carry graded forms with $\langle\varphi(a),\varphi(b)\rangle_W=\langle a,Lb\rangle_V$, and (c) $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign. Then $L^i:V^{-i}\to V^i$ is injective for all $i\ge0$, and if $\dim V^i=\dim V^{-i}$ for all $i$ then $L$ satisfies hL on $V$.

(3) **Sign bookkeeping.** If in (2) the lowest degree of $W$ is $-\ell$ and of $V$ is $-(\ell+1)$, then the Lefschetz form on $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ is $\pm$definite with the same sign as on $W^{-\ell}$, so if $V$ satisfies HR with the standard sign then $V$ has the standard sign if and only if $W$ does.

(4) **Degenerate shifted case.** Let the form on $H$ not be assumed non-degenerate and suppose $L^i:H^{-d-i}\to H^{-d+i}$ is an isomorphism for all $i\ge0$ with $d$ a positive integer. Then the Lefschetz form $(h,h')_L^{-i}=\langle h,L^ih'\rangle$ on $H^{-i}$ is identically zero for every $i\ge0$.

(5) **Stable-subspace lemma.** If $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ satisfies hL and HR and $V\subseteq H$ is an $L$-stable graded subspace with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$, then the restricted operator and form satisfy hL and HR on $V$ with the ambient degree-by-degree signs; the restricted form is non-degenerate, and its standard global sign agrees with the ambient standard sign if the lowest nonzero degrees agree.

**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=\underline H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form when $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here $d=\ell(x)$ by the proved normalized degree bounds. The property $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ always denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on $\overline{B_x^R}$, independently of $\mathrm{S}(x)$. $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the conjunction of $\mathrm{S}(x)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations with the standard sign for this normalized intrinsic form; its existence and uniqueness, and the nonzero positive bottom value used for normalization, are proved in [[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires the general Hodge-Riemann relations above for the restricted intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.

derivations.claim: **The basis and cross blocks.** Assume $W\ne0$; the zero case has zero tensor product and is vacuous. For $i\ge0$, choose lifts $e_a\in B^{-i-1}$ of a basis of $W^{-i-1}$ orthogonal for its Lefschetz form, and lifts $p_b\in B^{-i+1}$ of a basis of $P_W^{-i+1}$; for $i=0$ the latter space is zero. Primitive decomposition (and $A:W^{-1}\to W^1$ when $i=0$) gives a basis $Ae_a,p_b$ of $W^{-i+1}$. These lifts can be included in a homogeneous right basis of $B$, so $\alpha(Ae_a),\beta(e_a),\alpha(p_b)$ reduce to a basis of $V^{-i}$, where $V=\overline{BB_s}$. By [F1]–[F2], $L_\zeta\beta(y)=\beta(Ay)$ after reduction, the $\beta$–$\beta$ Lefschetz block is zero, and $\langle\alpha(x),L_\zeta^i\beta(y)\rangle=\langle x,A^iy\rangle_W$. Consequently the $\alpha(Ae)$–$\beta(e)$ block is the invertible diagonal matrix $J=(\langle e_a,A^{i+1}e_b\rangle_W)$, while the $\alpha(p)$–$\beta(e)$ block is zero, since $A^ip=0$ for primitives in degree $-i+1$.

**The signature comparison.** For nonzero $W$, let its lowest degree be $-d$ and put $b_i=\dim W^{-i}$ for integer $i$, so $b_{-i}=b_i$. For any $V$ as in the comparison statement put $v_i=\dim V^{-i}=b_{i-1}+b_{i+1}$. Under hL, its primitive dimensions are $p_i^V=v_i-v_{i+2}=b_{i-1}-b_{i+3}$, and $p_i^W=b_i-b_{i+2}$ for $i\ge0$. The standard-HR signature required on $V^{-i}$ is the finite sum $\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^{(d+1-i-2k)/2}p_{i+2k}^V$, in the occurring parity. Substitution and cancellation give $(-1)^{(d+1-i)/2}(b_{i-1}-b_{i+1})$ for $i\ge1$, exactly the signature of the primitive form on $P_W^{-i+1}$. For $i=0$ it is zero, since $b_{-1}=b_1$, matching $P_W^1=0$. By [F3] these signatures, together with hL, are equivalent to standard HR on $V$, proving both directions of the comparison. If $W=0$, the dimension identity forces $V=0$ and both sides are vacuous.

**The hyperbolic blocks.** The Lefschetz matrix on $V^{-i}$ therefore has form $\begin{pmatrix}C&J&E\\J&0&0\\E^{\mathsf T}&0&Q_\zeta\end{pmatrix}$. Subtracting suitable vectors from the $\beta$ block from the $\alpha(p)$ block kills $E$ without changing $Q_\zeta$; replacing the first block by itself minus one half of the corresponding $J^{-1}C$ combination of the second kills $C$. This gives a congruence to $\begin{pmatrix}0&J&0\\J&0&0\\0&0&Q_\zeta\end{pmatrix}$. The first two blocks are non-degenerate with equal positive and negative inertia. Thus the full matrix is non-degenerate exactly when $Q_\zeta$ is, and its signature is that of $Q_\zeta$. For $i=0$, $Q_\zeta$ is empty, so the matrix is already non-degenerate of signature zero for every parameter.

**The primitive block for $i>0$.** For the chosen lifts $p,q$ of degree $-i+1$, binomial expansion and [F1] give $\langle\alpha(p),L_\zeta^i\alpha(q)\rangle=\sum_{j=0}^i\binom{i}{j}\zeta^j\partial_s(\langle p,A^{i-j}q\rangle_B\rho^j)$ before reduction. The polynomial $\langle p,A^{i-j}q\rangle_B$ has degree $2-2j$: it vanishes for $j\ge2$, and for $j=1$ it is constant. Since $\partial_s\rho=\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$, reduction yields $Q_\zeta=Q_0+\zeta i\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)Q$, where $Q$ is the definite primitive Lefschetz matrix on $P_W^{-i+1}$. If this space is zero the block is empty. Otherwise $i>0$ and $\zeta^{-1}Q_\zeta$ tends to the definite matrix $i\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)Q$; symmetric elimination near that matrix preserves the pivot signs by [F3]. Hence for sufficiently large $\zeta$, $Q_\zeta$ is definite with the signature of $Q$. There are only finitely many nonzero graded pieces, so one bound on $\zeta$ works for all of them.

**Large parameters.** Steps 2.1–3.1 make every Lefschetz form on $V^{-i}$ non-degenerate for all sufficiently large parameters, so [F3] gives hL. Their signatures are precisely the primitive signatures of $W$; step 1.2 gives HR with the standard sign on $V$. This proves the large-parameter assertion, including the empty primitive blocks and $i=0$.

**Deformation principle.** On any compact interval joining $\zeta_0$ to another nonnegative parameter, the polynomial family $L_\zeta$ is continuous. If hL holds throughout, [F3] transfers HR from $\zeta_0$ to that parameter. When HR$(x)$ holds, step 4.1 supplies a large positive $\zeta_0$; otherwise the more general corollary assumes one such parameter. This proves both corollaries and completes the argument without choice.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 1.2 treat W=0 and V=0; step 2.1 treats the empty primitive block at i=0.
Step 5.1 transfers HR to zeta=0 only under hL throughout the joining interval; hL at zero is not asserted by the large-parameter theorem alone.
Step 2.1 and step 3.1: At i=0, P_W^1=0 and the Lefschetz matrix is hyperbolic; at i=1 the Q growth is rho(alpha_s^vee)Q and nonempty primitives have the prescribed sign.
Step 2.1 proves nondegeneracy iff Q_zeta is nondegenerate; 3.1 gives eventual definiteness for i>0, and i=0 has empty Q. The given ambient form is nondegenerate.
Step 3.1 covers sufficiently large zeta with one bound over finite support; step 5.1 covers any nonnegative parameter only under hL on the whole compact joining interval.
Step 1.1 and step 3.1: Only finitely many homogeneous/orthogonal bases of finite-dimensional spaces are chosen; no AC.
Step 1.2 substitutes primitive dimensions in the standard-HR signature sum and telescopes to the primitive W signature, including zero at i=0.
The same step 1.2, using primitive decomposition and hL, forces the correct primitive signatures by subtraction; definite signs follow from inertia, not nondegeneracy alone.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, let $B_x$ be the normalized indecomposable bimodule classified by its top support. With right dual $DM=\operatorname{Hom}_{-R}^{\bullet}(M,R)$, one has $DB_x\cong B_x$. Its right reduction has degrees only in $[-\ell(x),\ell(x)]$, all congruent to $\ell(x)$ modulo two, and the two extremal dimensions are one. Hence its reduced graded dimensions are symmetric. Every Bott-Samelson word has a graded perfect symmetric invariant trace form. These assertions assume neither the Kazhdan-Lusztig character conjecture nor hard Lefschetz.

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

**The setting.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$ with $xs>x$, and
$y<xs$ in the Bruhat order; assume $\mathrm{S}(z)$ for all $z<xs$. Choose
reduced-word embeddings $B_y^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline y)$
and $B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$, and equip $B_y^R$,
$B_x^R$ with the positively normalized non-degenerate invariant forms obtained
by restriction, so that the bottom Lefschetz values are $+1$; equip
$M:=B_x^RB_s^R$ with the induced invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]. Under
$\mathrm{S}(y)$ and $\mathrm{S}(x)$ these forms exist and are unique up to
positive scalars, and the choices enter only through positive factors
([[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]).

**The local intersection form.** Let
$$E_y:=\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$$
be the finite-dimensional real space of degree-zero bimodule maps. For
$f,g\in E_y$ define the **local intersection form**
$$(f,g)^{x,s}_y:=g^*\circ f\ \in\ \operatorname{End}^0(B_y^R)=\mathbb R,$$
where $g^*:M\to B_y^R$ is the **adjoint** of $g$ with respect to the two
non-degenerate forms, uniquely characterized by
$\langle g(b),m\rangle_M=\langle b,g^*(m)\rangle_{B_y}$ for all $b\in B_y^R$,
$m\in M$; adjunction is the standard transpose operation of
[[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]] under the identifications
$B_y^R\to (B_y^R)^*$ and $M\to M^*$ induced by the forms
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]). The adjoint construction
identifies $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$ with
$\operatorname{Hom}^0(M,B_y^R)$.

**Basic properties.** The form $(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ is symmetric: the adjoint of
$g^*f$ is $f^*g$, and a scalar endomorphism of $B_y^R$ is self-adjoint for its
invariant form. It is $\mathbb R$-bilinear, and it changes only by a positive
scalar when the chosen normalized forms or reduced-word embeddings are varied:
scaling the form on $M$ by $a>0$ and the form on $B_y^R$ by $b>0$ scales
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ by $a/b$, and the invariant-form uniqueness lemma shows that any
two choices compare by positive scalars. Define
$$\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$$
to mean that $(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ is definite of sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$, respectively its negative, with the parity
convention of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]: when the
numerator is odd the corresponding primitive space is zero and the sign
condition is not used.

**Status.** The definition uses degree-zero Hom throughout; no statement
identifies the rank of the full graded Hom module with a Kazhdan-Lusztig
multiplication coefficient. The dimension of $E_y$ in terms of the
multiplication formula, and the equivalence of non-degeneracy of these forms
with the actual summand multiplicities of $M$, are proved in the detection
theorem later on this page; they are not part of this definition.

Fix $x,s$ with $xs>x$ and assume $\mathrm{S}(y)$ for every $y<xs$. Put $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and write the Kazhdan-Lusztig multiplication formula $\underline H_x\underline H_s=\underline H_{xs}+\sum_{y<xs}\mu_y\underline H_y$ with integer constants $\mu_y$. For each $y<xs$ let $E_y=\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$ carry the local intersection form of [[def-local-intersection-form-for-a-soergel-summand]]. Then:

(1) $\dim_{\mathbb R}E_y=\mu_y$, while the full graded Hom module has graded rank $\langle\underline H_y,\underline H_x\underline H_s\rangle$, generally not $\mu_y$;

(2) the following are equivalent: $\mathrm{S}(xs)$; non-degeneracy of every local intersection form on $E_y$, $y<xs$; perfection of every degree-zero composition pairing $E_y\times\operatorname{Hom}^0(M,B_y^R)\to\operatorname{End}^0(B_y^R)=\mathbb R$; and equality of the actual multiplicity $a_y$ of $B_y^R$ in $M$ with $\mu_y$ for every $y<xs$.

The unconditional top summand is $B_{xs}$ with multiplicity one, and under $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ all remaining summands are unshifted $B_y^R$. No positivity of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials or conjecture at $xs$ is assumed.

derivations.claim: **The exact sequence and the degree-zero isomorphism.** The top support layer gives a short exact sequence $0\to\Delta_y\to B_y^R\to Q\to0$ of $\Delta$-filtered modules, and $\operatorname{Hom}(-,M)$ is left exact, so $0\to\operatorname{Hom}(Q,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}(B_y^R,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_y,M)$ is exact. By [F1] the three graded Hom spaces are free over $S$ and their graded ranks are additive in the $\Delta$-characters: $\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(B_y^R,M)=\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(Q,M)+\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_y,M)$ as polynomials. By [F2] all $v$-powers of $\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(Q,M)$ are positive, so the degree-$\le0$ part of the map $\operatorname{Hom}(B_y^R,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_y,M)$ is injective; comparing Hilbert series degree by degree, the two free modules have equal dimension in each degree $\le0$ after restriction, and the injective degreewise map is therefore an isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}^{\le0}(B_y^R,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}^{\le0}(\Delta_y,M)$. In particular restriction of degree-zero Hom is an isomorphism, and no full graded isomorphism is asserted.

**Evaluation at the top and then at the bottom.** Let $c\in B_y$ be the image of the homogeneous generator of $\Delta_y\subseteq B_y$. Its reduction spans $\overline{B_y}^{\ell(y)}$: the top-layer right splitting and image equality of [F3] make its reduction nonzero. By step 1.1 restriction is an isomorphism in degree zero, so evaluation at $c$ identifies the Hom space with $(\Gamma_yM)^{\ell(y)}$, which injects into $\overline M^{\ell(y)}$ by [F3]. Thus $f\mapsto\overline{f(c)}$ is injective. Hard Lefschetz on $B_y$, part of $HR(y)$, says that $\rho^{\ell(y)}c_{\mathrm{bot}}$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of $\overline c$ in that one-dimensional top degree. Therefore $\rho^{\ell(y)}f(c_{\mathrm{bot}})$ is the same nonzero scalar multiple of $\overline{f(c)}$. If bottom evaluation vanished then top evaluation would vanish, forcing $f=0$. Finally the degree bound $\overline{B_y}^{\ell(y)+2}=0$ gives $\rho^{\ell(y)+1}c_{\mathrm{bot}}=0$; bimodule linearity makes the image primitive. This proves (1), without asserting that the multiplicity space $(\Gamma_yM)^{\ell(y)}$ is one dimensional.

**The isometry.** For $f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$, the local form is $(f,g)^{x,s}_y=g^*\circ f$, a scalar endomorphism of $B_y^R$; by the normalization of [F4], $N(f,g)^{x,s}_y=\langle g^*(f(c_{\mathrm{bot}})),\rho^{\ell(y)}c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle_{B_y}$, and adjointness of $g^*$ gives $\langle f(c_{\mathrm{bot}}),\rho^{\ell(y)}g(c_{\mathrm{bot}})\rangle_M=(\mathrm{ev}(f),\mathrm{ev}(g))^{-\ell(y)}_\rho$, by definition of the Lefschetz form. The factor $N$ is positive by [F4]. This proves (2).

**From HR to the character (3).** Assume HR$(x,s)$. Since the operator $L_0$ on $\overline M$ has $P^{-\ell(y)}_\rho$ as a primitive subspace and HR makes the Lefschetz form on it definite, the restriction of this form to the image $\mathrm{ev}(E_y)$ is non-degenerate; by the isometry of step 3.1 with the positive factor $N$, the local intersection form on $E_y$ is non-degenerate. This holds for every $y<xs$, so the detection theorem [F5], whose hypothesis $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ is available, gives $\mathrm{S}(xs)$. This proves (3) and completes the lemma.

The degree endpoints structure the argument: step 1.1 uses the lowest degree of the top layer, step 2.1 identifies the image precisely in that degree, and step 4.1 closes the argument in the lowest primitive degree.

(1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

(1) **Family lemma.** Let $L_t$, $t\in[a,b]$, be a continuous family of symmetric degree-two operators on $H$, each satisfying hL, and suppose $L_{t_0}$ satisfies HR with the standard sign for one $t_0\in[a,b]$. Then every $L_t$ satisfies HR with the standard sign; in the application the family is $L_\zeta$, $\zeta\ge0$, which is polynomial (hence continuous) in $\zeta$.

(2) **Weak-Lefschetz substitute.** Let $\varphi:V\to W(1)$ be a map of graded $R[L]$-modules such that (a) $\varphi$ is injective in degrees $\le-1$, (b) $V,W$ carry graded forms with $\langle\varphi(a),\varphi(b)\rangle_W=\langle a,Lb\rangle_V$, and (c) $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign. Then $L^i:V^{-i}\to V^i$ is injective for all $i\ge0$, and if $\dim V^i=\dim V^{-i}$ for all $i$ then $L$ satisfies hL on $V$.

(3) **Sign bookkeeping.** If in (2) the lowest degree of $W$ is $-\ell$ and of $V$ is $-(\ell+1)$, then the Lefschetz form on $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ is $\pm$definite with the same sign as on $W^{-\ell}$, so if $V$ satisfies HR with the standard sign then $V$ has the standard sign if and only if $W$ does.

(4) **Degenerate shifted case.** Let the form on $H$ not be assumed non-degenerate and suppose $L^i:H^{-d-i}\to H^{-d+i}$ is an isomorphism for all $i\ge0$ with $d$ a positive integer. Then the Lefschetz form $(h,h')_L^{-i}=\langle h,L^ih'\rangle$ on $H^{-i}$ is identically zero for every $i\ge0$.

(5) **Stable-subspace lemma.** If $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ satisfies hL and HR and $V\subseteq H$ is an $L$-stable graded subspace with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$, then the restricted operator and form satisfy hL and HR on $V$ with the ambient degree-by-degree signs; the restricted form is non-degenerate, and its standard global sign agrees with the ambient standard sign if the lowest nonzero degrees agree.

derivations.claim: **Restriction of hard Lefschetz (a).** The inclusion $i:B_{xs}^R\to M$ and the projection $\pi:M\to B_{xs}^R$ of the summand are degree-zero bimodule maps, and they commute with left multiplication by $\rho$, since left multiplication by a central element is a bimodule endomorphism; after right reduction they remain a split inclusion and projection of the finite-dimensional real spaces. Hence the operator $L_0^i$ on $\overline M$ is block diagonal with respect to the decomposition of $\overline M$ into the summand and its complement, and each block is the corresponding power of the restricted operator. If $L_0^i$ is an isomorphism, then its inverse commutes with the block decomposition, so each diagonal block is invertible; in particular the block $\overline{B_{xs}^R}^{-i}\to\overline{B_{xs}^R}^{i}$ is an isomorphism. This holds for every $i\ge0$, which is $\mathrm{hL}(xs)$.

**The converse under the character hypotheses (b).** Assume $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(y)$ for all $y<xs$. By [F1] the decomposition $M=B_{xs}^R\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{R,a_y}$ has no shifts, and for $i<xs$ we have $\mathrm{S}(y)$; the module $B_{xs}^R$ is self-dual with symmetric Betti numbers, and by the comparison lemma the same holds for every lower summand. If $\mathrm{hL}(xs)$ holds, the block of $L_0^i$ on $B_{xs}^R$ is invertible; by hypothesis each lower block $B_y^R$ is invertible (hL$(y)$), and no other summands occur; therefore every diagonal block is invertible, so $L_0^i$ is invertible, which is $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$. This proves the equivalence.

**Restriction of HR (c).** Assume $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$, that is, HR for the restriction of the intersection form over a fixed reduced-word embedding of $\underline x$ and a fixed induced form of $M$; the summand $B_{xs}^R$ has symmetric Betti numbers by self-duality, and the inclusion is $L_0$-stable. Applying the stable-subspace lemma [F2] to $V=\overline{B_{xs}^R}$ inside $\overline M$ gives that the restricted operator and form satisfy hL and HR with the ambient signs; since the lowest degree of $B_{xs}^R$ equals the lowest degree $-\ell(xs)$ of $M$, the ambient standard sign is the standard sign of $B_{xs}^R$. Once $\mathrm{S}(xs)$ is known, [F3] identifies the restricted form with a positive multiple of the normalized intrinsic form, and $\mathrm{HR}(xs)$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(xs)$ follow with no change of signs.

**General stable subspaces (d).** The two assertions about $L_0$-stable subspaces with symmetric Betti numbers and $L_0$-stable direct summands are exactly the stable-subspace lemma [F2]; they apply to any $L_0$-stable subspace and do not use that $V$ is a tensor summand. A positive deformation $L_\zeta$ with $\zeta>0$ preserves a summand only when the summand's projector commutes with the middle-position operator, which is not automatic; when it does not, the restriction of $L_\zeta$ to the summand is not defined as an operator on the reduced summand, so no positive-parameter restriction statement is made. In particular no step identifies the restriction of $L_\zeta$ with left multiplication by $\rho$. This proves (d) and completes the lemma.

The same argument with the factors exchanged gives

of [[lem-rouquier-derived-comparisons-give-unique-normalized-homotopy-maps]]

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

**The construction.** For a signed word
$$\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},\qquad \epsilon_k\in\{\pm1\},\ 1\le i_k\le n-1,$$
put
$$F(\sigma):=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},$$
the iterated signed tensor totalization of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]] of
the Rouquier generator complexes of
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], bracketed left to
right; the empty word ($r=0$) is sent to the unit complex $R$ concentrated in
cohomological degree $0$. This is the **Rouquier complex of the word**. When
$\epsilon_k=+1$ the letter contributes the positive complex $F_{i_k}$ and when
$\epsilon_k=-1$ it contributes $F_{i_k}^{-1}$.

**Structure.** $F(\sigma)$ is a bounded cochain complex of graded
$(R,R)$-bimodules with degree-zero differentials, concentrated in cohomological
degrees $-r_-,\ldots,r_+$, where $r_-$ and $r_+$ count the negative and
positive letters: the term $F(\sigma)^m$ is the direct sum of the
$\binom{r}{m+r_-}$ tensor products of one term of each factor, since the
minimal choice has degree $-r_-$ and each upper-term choice adds one. It carries a
cohomological degree and an internal grading, and the differential is the
Koszul totalization differential. A positive letter contributes its unit term
$R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and the internal shift $(1)$ to that term; a
negative letter contributes its unit term $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$
and the internal shift $(-1)$. Every term is a finite direct sum of finite tensor products of copies
of $R(\pm1)$ and $B_i$, hence is finite free on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]), so each term
is finite graded projective as a left module and as a right module and $F(\sigma)$ defines a
derived tensor functor by
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]].

**Status of the notation.** The notation records the chosen word $(\sigma)$
together with the chosen bracket; it asserts nothing about independence of the
word, of the sign normalization or of the bracketing. That the homotopy class
of $F(\sigma)$ depends only on the braid represented by $\sigma$ is the content
of [[thm-rouquier-complex-is-well-defined-up-to-canonical-homotopy-equivalence]],
whose proof uses the braid relations of the generator complexes and could not be
stated before those relations were proved.

differ from $F_i$ and $F_i^{-1}$ by homological or internal shifts, so any
