Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; every $p_{y,w}$ has integer coefficients and fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

**The category and its radical.** Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ be the real
graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad \tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad \tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside
which the Rouquier complexes of the next items are shown to lie, following the
orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.

(1) The quotient $\mathcal B^{ss}$ is semisimple with simple classes $B_x(k)$ and endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$, and $q$ reflects isomorphisms.

(2) Every bounded complex of $\mathcal B$ has a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, and any two minimal models are isomorphic as complexes.

(3) Every direct summand of a perverse (respectively p-split) bimodule is perverse (respectively p-split).

(4) For perverse $M,N$ one has $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N(-i))=0$ for $i>0$.

(5) The perverse cuts on p-split bimodules are independent of the chosen decomposition and are preserved by every morphism.

(6) The definitions of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ can equivalently be tested on the minimal model, and both classes are closed under extensions in distinguished triangles.

Let $\underline x$ be a reduced expression for $x\in S_n$ and let $F_{\underline x}$ be the Rouquier complex $F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$ (or its minimal subcomplex). Then for every $y\in S_n$ there is an isomorphism in the homotopy category of graded bimodules
$$\Gamma_{\ge y}(F_{\underline x})/\Gamma_{>y}(F_{\underline x})\;\cong\;\begin{cases}\Delta_x,&y=x,\\0,&y\ne x,\end{cases}$$
where $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. Equivalently: the Bruhat support subquotient of a positive Rouquier complex is contractible except in the top layer $\Delta_x$; $F_{\underline x}$ is $\Delta$-split in the sense that each of its support subquotients is a direct sum of standard bimodules, and the top layer is a single $\Delta_x$. No positivity of characters and no assumption $\mathrm{S}$ is used; the statement is unconditional for every finite type-$A$ Coxeter group and the coordinate reflection realization.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

derivations.claim: **Base of the induction.** [base] For $x=e$ the Rouquier complex is the unit $S$ concentrated in cohomological degree $0$, so $^0F_e=S=B_e$, there is no term of index $i\ge1$, both perverse bounds hold trivially, and the only nonzero inverse coefficient is $g_{e,e}=1$; for $x=s_i$ the complex $F_{s_i}=[B_{s_i}^R\to S(1)]$ has $^0F_{s_i}=B_{s_i}$ and $^1F_{s_i}=S(1)=B_e^R(1)$ and no other term, so $m_{e,1}=1$ with $\ell(s_i)-\ell(e)=1\equiv1\pmod2$, $B_{s_i}$ is perverse by $\mathrm S(s_i)$ and $S(1)$ is the shift of the perverse unit, so $F_{s_i}\in pK^b_{\ge0}\cap pK^b_{\le0}$ and $g_{s_i,s_i}=1$, $g_{e,s_i}=-v$.

**Induction hypothesis and the last letter.** [ih] Fix $x\ne e$, write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ with $m\ge1$ and put $y=s_1\cdots s_{m-1}$, $s=s_m$, so that $x=ys$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(y)+1$; the hypothesis $\mathrm S(\le x)$ contains $\mathrm S(\le y)$, and we assume the three assertions of the statement for $y$: $^0F_y=B_y$, $^iF_y=\bigoplus_{z<y}B_z(i)^{m^y_{z,i}}$ for $i\ge1$, and $F_y\in pK^b_{\ge0}\cap pK^b_{\le0}$. By [F1], $F_x\cong F_yF_s$ in $K^b$.

**Descent contraction.** Let $z$ and a simple reflection $s$ satisfy $zs<z$ and $\mathrm S(z)$; then $B_zF_s\cong B_z(-1)$ in $K^b$. Indeed, by [F2] the two-term complex $B_zF_s$ has terms $B_zB_s=B_z(1)\oplus B_z(-1)$ in degree $0$ and $B_z(1)$ in degree $1$, with differential $d=(\delta,\eta)$ where $\delta\in\operatorname{End}^0(B_z(1))=\operatorname{End}^0(B_z)=\mathbb R$ by [F2] and [F6]. If $\delta=0$ then $B_zF_s$ is the direct sum of the two nonzero complexes $[B_z(1)\to0]$ and $[B_z(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \eta\ }B_z(1)]$, contradicting the indecomposability of $B_zF_s$, which is the image of the indecomposable $B_z$ under the equivalence $-\otimes F_s$; hence $\delta\ne0$ is an isomorphism, homological Gaussian elimination cancels the contractible two-term complex $B_z(1)\cong B_z(1)$, and the remainder is $B_z(-1)$ concentrated in degree $0$.

**Top support and the Euler character.** Every positive-degree term of the word complex omits at least one letter, so no such term has the $x$ graph by [F3]. The degree-zero term is its reduced word, whose top summand is exactly $B_x$ unshifted and once. Gaussian minimalization cannot remove it, since no target term has its label. Thus in the minimal complex $m^0_{x,0}=1$ and every other $m^i_{x,k}$ is zero, by actual support rather than alternating cancellation. Character additivity makes its Euler character unchanged by removing a contractible pair. The generator recursion and shift rule in [F3] give $\operatorname{ch}(F_zF_s)=\operatorname{ch}(F_z)(\underline H_s-v)$ degree by degree. Iterating along the reduced word therefore gives Euler character $H_x$. Under the stated $S(\le x)$, expanding each actual summand character in the KL basis yields $\sum_{i,k}(-1)^im^i_{w,k}v^k=g_{w,x}$. This equality is used only for the Euler coefficients, after the support proof of the top multiplicity.

**Ascent perverse bound.** Let $z\le y$ and a simple reflection $s$ satisfy $zs>z$; then $B_zF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$. Indeed, $\mathrm S(u)$ holds for every $u<zs$, because $u<zs\le x$ implies $u<x$; so [F2] gives the unshifted decomposition $B_zB_s=B_{zs}\oplus\bigoplus_{u<zs}B_u^{a_u}$, whose summands are perverse by $\mathrm S(zs)$ and $\mathrm S(u)$, while the second term $B_z(1)$ of $B_zF_s=[B_zB_s\to B_z(1)]$ is the internal shift of the perverse $B_z$ sitting in cohomological degree $1$; thus the chosen representative has p-split terms and satisfies $\tau_{<0}(B_zB_s)=0$ and $\tau_{<-1}(B_z(1))=0$, which is membership in $pK^b_{\ge0}$ by [F5].

**Shift propagation.** Assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$ and let $F_x$ be minimal. If $^iF_x$ contains a summand $B_z(j)$ with $z<x$, then $^{i-1}F_x$ contains a summand $B_{z'}(j')$ with $z'>z$ and $j'<j$. First, components of the differential into summands of shift $k<j$ vanish: a degree-zero map $B_z(j)\to B_u(k)$ is an element of $\operatorname{Hom}^{k-j}(B_z,B_u)$, which is zero for $k<j$ since the graded Hom space has no negative-degree part by [F6]; components with $k=j$ are zero for $u\ne z$ by [F6] and are scalars for $u=z$, and a nonzero scalar component would make $B_z(j)$ a contractible summand of the minimal complex, so all such components vanish as well; hence $d(B_z(j))$ lies in the sum of the summands of $^{i+1}F_x$ with shift $k>j$. Second, if a summand $B_u(k)$ of $^{i-1}F_x$ maps nontrivially to $B_z(j)$, then $k<j$: a degree-zero map $B_u(k)\to B_z(j)$ lies in $\operatorname{Hom}^{j-k}(B_u,B_z)$, which vanishes for $j<k$, and for $j=k$ it vanishes for $u\ne z$ and is a scalar for $u=z$, the nonzero case again being excluded by minimality. Third, apply the support cutoff $\Gamma_{\ge z/>z}$ and reduce its free graph modules modulo $R_+$. Since $z<x$, its complex is contractible by [F5], hence this reduced finite-dimensional complex is exact. The chosen top layer $\Delta_z(j)$ of $B_z(j)$ is a nonzero homogeneous basis vector. Every outgoing target has shift $k>j$, and its $z$ layer has shift $k+d$ with $d\ge0$ by KL triangularity. A map from the chosen generator into it consequently has positive-degree coefficient, so vanishes after reduction. The chosen vector is a cycle and must therefore be an incoming boundary. Some incoming component has a nonzero constant coefficient onto it, so some $B_{z'}(j')$ in degree $i-1$ has a $z$ layer with $j'+d=j$. The underlying differential component is nonzero, and the preceding Hom estimate gives $j'<j$. Since $d=0$ for label $z$ itself, this requires $z'>z$. This proves shift propagation without using an Euler identity to recover multiplicities.

**The perverse lower bound for $F_x$.** Use the stupid filtration $w_{\ge k}F_y$ of the minimal complex $F_y$, with distinguished triangles $w_{\ge k+1}F_y\to w_{\ge k}F_y\to{}^kF_y[-k]\to$ and $w_{\ge\ell(y)+1}F_y=0$; tensoring with the invertible $F_s$ preserves distinguished triangles. We prove $(w_{\ge k}F_y)F_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ by descending induction on $k$: for $k=\ell(y)+1$ the object is $0$; assume it for $k+1$. By [ih] and step 2.1, $^kF_y$ is a direct sum of summands $B_z(k)$ with $z\le y$ (with $z=y$ only for $k=0$), so $(^kF_y)F_s[-k]$ is a direct sum of copies of $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]$. If $zs>z$ then $B_zF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ by step 4.1, and its internal shift $(k)$ and homological shift $[-k]$ place every summand $B_u(\ell)$ occurring in cohomological degree $i$ into degree $i+k$ with internal shift $\ell+k\le i+k$, so $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]\in pK^b_{\ge0}$; if $zs<z$  then step 3.1 gives $B_zF_s\cong B_z(-1)$, so $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]\cong B_z(k-1)[-k]$, a perverse object with internal shift $k-1$ in cohomological degree $k$, again in $pK^b_{\ge0}$. Extension closure of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ in the tensored triangles gives $(w_{\ge k}F_y)F_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$, and at $k=0$ we obtain $F_yF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$; by step 2.1 this is $F_x\in pK^b_{\ge0}$.

**The top term and the perverse upper bound.** If $^0F_x$ contained a summand $B_z(j)$ with $z<x$, then step 4.2 with $i=0$ would produce a summand of $^{-1}F_x=0$, which is impossible; hence every summand of $^0F_x$ has label $x$, and by step 3.2 ($m^0_{x,0}=1$ and $m^0_{x,k}=0$ for $k\ne0$) we get $^0F_x=B_x$, which proves (1). Now suppose $i\ge1$ and $^iF_x$ has a summand $B_z(k)$ with $k<i$; if $z=x$ this contradicts $m^i_{x,k}=0$ from step 3.2, so $z<x$, and step 4.2 produces a summand $B_{z'}(k')$ of $^{i-1}F_x$ with $k'<k<i$. This summand is again of the forbidden type: if $z'=x$ then $m^{i-1}_{x,k'}=0$ whenever $i-1\ge1$, while for $i-1=0$ it contradicts $^0F_x=B_x$ because $k'<0$; otherwise $z'<x$ and step 4.2 applies again. Iterating this descent in the homological degree we reach a summand of $^0F_x$ with negative internal shift, contradicting $^0F_x=B_x$. Hence every summand of $^iF_x$ has internal shift $\ge i$ for $i\ge1$, which together with $F_x\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ from step 5.1 gives $F_x\in pK^b_{\le0}$; since for $i\ge1$ the label $x$ does not occur by step 3.2, we obtain $^iF_x=\bigoplus_{z<x}B_z(i)^{m_{z,i}}$ with $m_{z,i}:=m^i_{z,i}$, which is (2).

**Inversion of the Kazhdan-Lusztig transition matrix.** Let the two bases be related by $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}h_{y,w}H_y$ and $H_w=\sum_{y\le w}g_{y,w}\underline H_y$ as in [F4]; substituting the first expansion into the second gives $\sum_{y\le z\le w}h_{y,z}g_{z,w}=\delta_{y,w}$. Hence $g_{w,w}=1$ and, for $y<w$, $g_{y,w}=-\sum_{y<z\le w}h_{y,z}g_{z,w}$. We prove $g_{y,w}\in v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by descending induction on $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: for $y=w$ this is $1\in v^0\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$, and for $y<w$ each $h_{y,z}$ lies in $v^{\ell(z)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by [F4] and each $g_{z,w}$ with $y<z\le w$ lies in $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(z)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by the hypothesis of the induction, so each product lies in $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ and the finite sum does too.

**Parity and positivity of the inverse coefficients.** By step 3.2 and step 6.1 the multiplicities appearing in $g_{z,x}=\sum_i(-1)^im_{z,i}v^i$ are exactly the multiplicities of the linear complex $F_x$, and by step 7.1 we have $g_{z,x}\in v^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; therefore the coefficient $(-1)^im_{z,i}$ of $v^i$ can be nonzero only when $i\equiv\ell(x)-\ell(z)\pmod2$, which is the parity clause of (3). For such $i$ the sign $(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)+i}$ equals $+1$, so $(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)}g_{z,x}=\sum_i(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)+i}m_{z,i}v^i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}[v^{\pm1}]$, and the coefficients are the nonnegative multiplicities $m_{z,i}$. This proves (3) and, with (1) and (2), completes the induction.

boundaries.evidence: The empty word is the base of the induction and is discharged at the start of step 1.1: the complex is the unit in degree zero, there are no higher terms, both perverse bounds are trivial and the multiplicity statement is vacuous.

The degree-zero term is pinned down in step 6.1: a lower summand there would propagate to a summand of the term in degree -1, which is zero, so the top term is exactly the indecomposable; the vanishing of the negative terms is what drives the argument.

The unit-length word is the first nontrivial instance of the induction: step 2.1 sets up the last letter with the induction hypothesis for the shorter word, and step 3.1 handles the descent contraction used when that letter lowers the length.

Non-reduced or non-minimal representatives are excluded by the hypotheses rather than assumed away: step 5.1 splits off the contractible summand of the perverse truncation and step 3.1 performs the descent contraction only across an invertible differential block.

The two perverse bounds are the grading endpoints: step 4.1 proves the lower bound for the ascent complex, step 6.1 the upper bound, and linearity pins each summand of the degree-indexed term at exactly the matching internal shift.
Choice-free: the induction runs over the finite set of permutations, and every cancellation in steps 3.1 and 5.1 is performed on an explicitly invertible block.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is a list of structural conclusions about a minimal complex; it states no equivalence, so there is no forward direction to discharge.
No converse is claimed: the linearity and multiplicity statements are proved directly from the character hypotheses, not as one side of a biconditional.

citations.quote: Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ be
the split Grothendieck ring of the type-A Soergel category
([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]) and let
$h_\Delta,h_\nabla$ be the intrinsic $\Delta$- and $\nabla$-multiplicity
characters of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]],
which by [[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] are
well-defined functions of the bimodule and additive on direct sums, so that
they descend to $\mathbb Z$-linear maps on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$
with values in the Hecke algebra $H_{S_n}$ of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] whose normalized
generators are $H_i=v(T_i+1)$. Then:

1. $h_\Delta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebras
   $$h_\Delta:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad h_\Delta(XY)=h_\Delta(X)h_\Delta(Y),\qquad h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X),$$ that is
   $h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X)$, and $h_\Delta([B_i])=H_i$ for every simple
   reflection;
2. $h_\nabla$ is multiplicative, $h_\nabla(XY)=h_\nabla(X)h_\nabla(Y)$, and
   semilinear for the involution $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ of the coefficients:
   $h_\nabla(vX)=v^{-1}h_\nabla(X)$ and $h_\nabla([B_i])=H_i$; equivalently
   $h_\nabla=d\circ h_\Delta$, where $d$ is the semilinear algebra involution
   of $H_{S_n}$ determined by $d(v)=v^{-1}$ and $d(T_i)=T_i^{-1}$;
3. for every Bott–Samelson word $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ one has
   $h_\Delta(B_{\underline i})=h_\nabla(B_{\underline i})=H_{i_1}\cdots H_{i_r}$,
   and for every bimodule $M$ in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$ and simple reflection
   $s_i$ the simple-generator recursion
   $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$,
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$ holds; in the Elias–Williamson
   grading shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$
   and $h_\nabla$ by $v^{-1}$.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

**The setting.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$ with $xs>x$, and
$y<xs$ in the Bruhat order; assume $\mathrm{S}(z)$ for all $z<xs$. Choose
reduced-word embeddings $B_y^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline y)$
and $B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$, and equip $B_y^R$,
$B_x^R$ with the positively normalized non-degenerate invariant forms obtained
by restriction, so that the bottom Lefschetz values are $+1$; equip
$M:=B_x^RB_s^R$ with the induced invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]. Under
$\mathrm{S}(y)$ and $\mathrm{S}(x)$ these forms exist and are unique up to
positive scalars, and the choices enter only through positive factors
([[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]).

**The local intersection form.** Let
$$E_y:=\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$$
be the finite-dimensional real space of degree-zero bimodule maps. For
$f,g\in E_y$ define the **local intersection form**
$$(f,g)^{x,s}_y:=g^*\circ f\ \in\ \operatorname{End}^0(B_y^R)=\mathbb R,$$
where $g^*:M\to B_y^R$ is the **adjoint** of $g$ with respect to the two
non-degenerate forms, uniquely characterized by
$\langle g(b),m\rangle_M=\langle b,g^*(m)\rangle_{B_y}$ for all $b\in B_y^R$,
$m\in M$; adjunction is the standard transpose operation of
[[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]] under the identifications
$B_y^R\to (B_y^R)^*$ and $M\to M^*$ induced by the forms
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]). The adjoint construction
identifies $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$ with
$\operatorname{Hom}^0(M,B_y^R)$.

**Basic properties.** The form $(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ is symmetric: the adjoint of
$g^*f$ is $f^*g$, and a scalar endomorphism of $B_y^R$ is self-adjoint for its
invariant form. It is $\mathbb R$-bilinear, and it changes only by a positive
scalar when the chosen normalized forms or reduced-word embeddings are varied:
scaling the form on $M$ by $a>0$ and the form on $B_y^R$ by $b>0$ scales
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ by $a/b$, and the invariant-form uniqueness lemma shows that any
two choices compare by positive scalars. Define
$$\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$$
to mean that $(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ is definite of sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$, respectively its negative, with the parity
convention of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]: when the
numerator is odd the corresponding primitive space is zero and the sign
condition is not used.

**Status.** The definition uses degree-zero Hom throughout; no statement
identifies the rank of the full graded Hom module with a Kazhdan-Lusztig
multiplication coefficient. The dimension of $E_y$ in terms of the
multiplication formula, and the equivalence of non-degeneracy of these forms
with the actual summand multiplicities of $M$, are proved in the detection
theorem later on this page; they are not part of this definition.

**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=\underline H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form when $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here $d=\ell(x)$ by the proved normalized degree bounds. The property $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ always denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on $\overline{B_x^R}$, independently of $\mathrm{S}(x)$. $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the conjunction of $\mathrm{S}(x)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations with the standard sign for this normalized intrinsic form; its existence and uniqueness, and the nonzero positive bottom value used for normalization, are proved in [[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires the general Hodge-Riemann relations above for the restricted intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.

derivations.claim: **The dimension of $E_y$.** By [F1] and [F2] the graded rank of $\operatorname{Hom}(B_y^R,M)$ equals $\langle h_\Delta(B_y^R),h_\nabla(M)\rangle=\langle\underline H_y,\underline H_x\underline H_s\rangle$. Expanding $\underline H_x\underline H_s=\underline H_{xs}+\sum_{z<xs}\mu_z\underline H_z$ in the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and using the trace values of [F2], this rank equals $\sum_z\mu_z(\underline H_y,\underline H_z)$ up to the top term, whose contribution is $\delta_{y,xs}=0$ because $y<xs$; each $(\underline H_y,\underline H_z)$ lies in $v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $z\ne y$ and in $1+v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $z=y$. Hence the constant term of the graded rank is $\mu_y$, and since the graded rank lies in $\mathbb Z[v]$ with nonnegative $v$-powers, the degree-zero dimension is exactly the constant term: $\dim_{\mathbb R}E_y=\mu_y$. This is the first assertion of (1); the full graded rank is the polynomial displayed and has higher-degree terms in general, so it is not in general equal to the integer $\mu_y$.

**The top summand and the composition pairing.** By [F1], $M=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{R,a_y}$ with the top summand of multiplicity one. For $y<xs$, consider a composite $B_y^R\to M\to B_y^R$ factoring through a summand other than a copy of $B_y^R$; it cannot be a nonzero scalar multiple of the identity, because rescaling such a composite would exhibit a retraction splitting $B_y^R$ off that other summand, contradicting the uniqueness of the indecomposable label. Hence only the $a_y$ copies of $B_y^R$ contribute to the scalar-coordinate pairing, and the pairing matrix is the standard evaluation pairing of rank $a_y$; by the adjoint identification of [F3] the local intersection form has the same rank.

**Non-degeneracy and the multiplicity equalities.** By step 2.1 the local form on $E_y$ is non-degenerate if and only if its rank equals $\dim E_y$, i.e. $a_y=\mu_y$; by [F4] this is equivalent to non-degeneracy in the sense of trivial radical. Therefore non-degeneracy of every local form for all $y<xs$ is equivalent to the system of equalities $a_y=\mu_y$ for all $y<xs$, and the same rank comparison identifies this with perfection of the composition pairings.

**The character equivalence and conclusion.** By additivity of the character and $\operatorname{ch}(B_z)=\underline H_z$ for $z<xs$, the character of $B_{xs}$ is $\operatorname{ch}(M)-\sum_{y<xs}a_y\underline H_y=\underline H_{xs}+\sum_{y<xs}(\mu_y-a_y)\underline H_y$. Since the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis is a basis of the Hecke algebra, $\operatorname{ch}(B_{xs})=\underline H_{xs}$, i.e. $\mathrm{S}(xs)$, holds if and only if $\mu_y=a_y$ for every $y<xs$. Combining with step 3.1 gives the equivalence of all four conditions in (2).

Let $t,u$ be signed words for the same braid $v$. Then the normalized map
$$\gamma_{t,u}\colon F(t)\longrightarrow F(u)$$
of [[lem-rouquier-derived-comparisons-give-unique-normalized-homotopy-maps]]
is a canonical homotopy equivalence, natural with respect to the multiplication
maps: for every other braid $v'$ with chosen words $t',u'$, the diagrams
comparing $F(t)\otimes_RF(t')$ with $F(u)\otimes_RF(u')$ commute up to the
canonical associativity isomorphisms, and $\gamma_{t,u}$ is the unique homotopy
class with the prescribed derived image $c_{t,u}$. Consequently the object
$G_v$ of [[thm-rouquier-complexes-form-a-coherent-braid-group-action]] is
independent of the chosen representative up to canonical homotopy equivalence,
and the notation $F(\beta)$ for the Rouquier complex of a braid element is well
defined up to canonical isomorphism in $K^b(R^e\text{-grmod})$; this is an
isomorphism statement in the homotopy category, not an equality of complexes.

**The category and its radical.** Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ be the real
graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad \tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad \tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside
which the Rouquier complexes of the next items are shown to lie, following the
orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.

Let $X^\bullet$ be a cochain complex in an additive category with an
invertible-block decomposition
$d^n=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&\varphi\end{pmatrix}:A\oplus U\to B\oplus V$ and
Schur complement $\bar d=a-b\varphi^{-1}c$, as in
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]], and let
$\bar X^\bullet$ be the candidate reduction. Let $K$ be the two-term cochain
complex with $K^n=U$, $K^{n+1}=V$, $K^j=0$ for $j\notin\{n,n+1\}$ and
differential $d_K^n=\varphi$; write $\bar X\oplus K$ for the degreewise
biproduct.

1. The cochain map $T:X^\bullet\to\bar X^\bullet\oplus K$ with components
   $$T^j=1\ (j\notin\{n,n+1\}),\qquad T^n=R^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ \varphi^{-1}c&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^{n+1}=L=\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\varphi^{-1}\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}$$
   is an isomorphism of cochain complexes, with inverse the cochain map $T^{-1}$
   whose components are $1$ in degrees $j\notin\{n,n+1\}$, $R$ in degree $n$ and
   $L^{-1}$ in degree $n+1$.
2. $K$ is contractible, with contracting homotopy $k^{n+1}=\varphi^{-1}:V\to U$
   and $k^j=0$ for $j\ne n+1$.
3. $X^\bullet$ and $\bar X^\bullet$ are homotopy equivalent: the projection
   $\tilde p:\bar X\oplus K\to\bar X$ and the inclusion
   $\tilde\imath:\bar X\to\bar X\oplus K$ satisfy
   $\tilde p\tilde\imath=1$ and $1-\tilde\imath\tilde p=d\tilde h+\tilde h d$
   for the homotopy $\tilde h$ vanishing except in degree $n+1$, where
   $\tilde h^{n+1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&\varphi^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$, so that
   $p:=\tilde pT$ and $\imath:=T^{-1}\tilde\imath$ are homotopy inverse cochain
   maps.
4. The construction is a chain isomorphism followed by deletion of a
   contractible summand: it does not identify $X^\bullet$ with
   $\bar X^\bullet$ before that summand is split off, and in general $X^\bullet$
   and $\bar X^\bullet$ do not even have the same objects.

(1) The quotient $\mathcal B^{ss}$ is semisimple with simple classes $B_x(k)$ and endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$, and $q$ reflects isomorphisms.

(2) Every bounded complex of $\mathcal B$ has a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, and any two minimal models are isomorphic as complexes.

(3) Every direct summand of a perverse (respectively p-split) bimodule is perverse (respectively p-split).

(4) For perverse $M,N$ one has $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N(-i))=0$ for $i>0$.

(5) The perverse cuts on p-split bimodules are independent of the chosen decomposition and are preserved by every morphism.

(6) The definitions of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ can equivalently be tested on the minimal model, and both classes are closed under extensions in distinguished triangles.

derivations.claim: **The rank-one retraction.** In the right basis $(c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s)$ of $B_s^R$ we have $\varepsilon_s(c_{\mathrm{id}}a+c_sb)=a+b\alpha_s$ for $a,b\in S$. The section $\sigma(r)=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot r$ satisfies $\varepsilon_s\sigma(r)=r$, so $\varepsilon_s$ is split surjective and $B_s^R=\sigma(S(1))\oplus\ker(\varepsilon_s)$ as right $S$-modules; the subcomplex $\sigma(S(1))\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }S(1)$ of $F_s$ is contractible, and $\ker(\varepsilon_s)$ is a direct summand of the complex $F_s$ concentrated in degree $0$. The kernel is $\{c_{\mathrm{id}}(-\alpha_sb)+c_sb\}=\{(c_s-c_{\mathrm{id}}\alpha_s)b\}$, so it is free of rank one as a right $S$-module with generator $c_s-c_{\mathrm{id}}\alpha_s=(\alpha_s\otimes1-1\otimes\alpha_s)/2$ of internal degree $1$; hence $\ker(\varepsilon_s)\cong S(-1)$ as a graded right $S$-module and $F_s\simeq S(-1)$ in the homotopy category of complexes of graded right $S$-modules.

**The injectivity criterion.** Let $C$ be as in (2) and let $c\in\overline{C^0}$ be homogeneous of internal degree $D$ with $\overline{d^0}(c)=0$. Then $c$ is a cocycle, so it represents a class $[c]\in H^0(\overline C)$; since $H^{-1}(\overline C)=0$ and $C^{-1}=0$, the zeroth cohomology is the cokernel of no incoming map and $[c]$ vanishes if and only if $c$ lies in the image of $\overline{d^{-1}}$, which is zero because $C^{-1}=0$. Hence $[c]\ne0$ forces $D$ to be the single internal degree $d$ in which $H^0(\overline C)$ is concentrated; therefore a nonzero kernel element can occur only in degree $d$, and the map is injective in every other degree, in particular in degrees $\le d-1$. If $C'$ is homotopy equivalent to $C$ with $C'^{-1}=0$ and is obtained by cancelling contractible two-term summands whose source lies in positive cohomological degree, then $C'^0=C^0$ for the cancellation in degrees $\ge1$, the reductions $\overline{C'}$ and $\overline C$ are homotopy equivalent by [F3], so $H^{-1}(\overline{C'})=0$ and $H^0(\overline{C'})$ is concentrated in degree $d$, and the same argument applies to $C'$. This proves (2).

**The retraction for a reduced word.** Write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$. For $m=0$ the complex is $S$. For $m>0$, tensor the right-$S$-linear homotopy equivalence $F_{s_1}\simeq S(-1)$ of step 1.1 with the remaining bimodule complex $G=F_{s_2}\cdots F_{s_m}$. This is legitimate because the maps and homotopies on the first factor are right linear; signed totalization preserves the homotopy identities. As a complex of right modules, $S(-1)\otimes_S G\cong G(-1)$. Repeating on the first remaining factor gives $F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}\simeq S(-m)$. No left action is assigned to a right-module retraction and no right-linear map is tensored as a map on the second factor. Forgetting the left action of the bimodule homotopy equivalence from $F_x$ to this word complex proves (1). Applying the additive reduction functor preserves these homotopy identities, so the reduced cohomology is a single copy of $\mathbb R$ in internal degree $m$.

**Application to $F_xF_s$.** Let $xs>x$ and assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$. By [F2] the concatenated word is reduced for $xs$, so $F_xF_s\cong F_{xs}$ in $K^b$, and by step 2.1 applied to $xs$ the complex $F_{xs}$ is homotopy equivalent over right $S$-modules to $S(-\ell(xs))=S(-\ell(x)-1)$ concentrated in cohomological degree $0$. Hence $C:=F_xF_s$ satisfies the hypotheses of (2) with $d=\ell(x)+1$: it is bounded below, $C^{-1}=0$, and its reduction has $H^{-1}=0$ with $H^0$ one copy of $\mathbb R$ in internal degree $\ell(x)+1$. By step 1.2 the reduced first differential $\overline{d^0}$ is injective in internal degrees $\le\ell(x)$, which is (3); note that $F_xF_s$ has the terms $C^0=B_x^RB_s^R$ and $C^1={}^1F_xB_s\oplus B_x^R(1)$ by [F2], and that no minimality of $F_xF_s$ was used, only the homotopy equivalence with $F_{xs}$.

**Stability under cancellation and the descent caveat.** If the zero-parameter hard-Lefschetz proof cancels a contractible summand of $F_xF_s$ whose source lies in cohomological degree $\ge1$ (the shifted descent piece), the surviving complex $C'$ has $C'^{-1}=0$, is homotopy equivalent to $C$ and has $\overline{C'}$ homotopy equivalent to $\overline C$, so step 1.2 applies and the reduced first differential of $C'$ is still injective in internal degrees $\le\ell(x)$; this is the "splitting off contractible summands with zero degree-zero source" clause of (2). On the other hand the form identity $\langle b,L_\zeta b'\rangle=\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle_\gamma$ and the commutation $\varphi(L_\zeta b)=L\varphi(b)$ do not follow from the right-module retraction: they are identities between maps of bimodules involving the induced forms and the deleted-word factorization, and they must be verified in the hard-Lefschetz theorem using [F4]; for $\zeta=0$ on a descent summand the Lefschetz form of the shifted piece is identically zero, so the theorem restricts the weak-Lefschetz substitute to the kernel of $d_3$ instead of the whole target. This completes the proof of (3) and (4).

graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad \tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad \tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside

orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.

derivations.claim: **Base of the induction.** [base] For $x=e$ the complex is $F_e=S$, $m=0$, and for $j=0$ the space $^0F_e(0)=S$ satisfies hL and HR trivially: its lowest degree is $0$, the primitive subspace $P^0=\mathbb R$ carries the positive definite form $\langle1,1\rangle>0$, and $0\equiv-m+j\pmod4$, so the global sign is the standard one; there are no $j\ge1$ terms.

**Induction hypothesis and the last letter.** [ih] Fix $x\ne e$ and assume the statement for every $y<x$. Write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$, $y=s_1\cdots s_{m-1}$ and $s=s_m$, so that $x=ys$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(y)+1$ and $F_x$ is a summand of $F_yF_s$; fix an embedding $F_y\subseteq^{\oplus}F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_{m-1}}$ witnessing the induction hypothesis and use it to embed $F_x\subseteq^{\oplus}F_yF_s\subset F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$. For every $j$ this gives the embedding chain of [F1], $^jF_x(-j)\subseteq^{\oplus}{}^jF_yB_s(-j)\oplus{}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$, and the induction hypothesis applies to ${}^jF_y(-j)$ and to ${}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$ with the global signs indexed by $y$; by [F2] the $j$-th term of $F_x$ is linear.

**The decomposition of the middle term and orthogonality.** Under $\mathrm S(\le x)$ the comparison lemma gives a decomposition of the multiplicity space, so ${}^jF_y(-j)=\bigoplus_{z}V_z\otimes_\mathbb RB_z$ with degree-zero multiplicity spaces $V_z$; define $B^\uparrow=\bigoplus_{zs>z}V_z\otimes B_z$ and $B^\downarrow=\bigoplus_{zs<z}V_z\otimes B_z$, so that ${}^jF_y(-j)=B^\uparrow\oplus B^\downarrow$. The decomposition is orthogonal for the induced form because $\operatorname{Hom}(B^\uparrow,D B^\downarrow)=\operatorname{Hom}(B^\downarrow,DB^\uparrow)=0$ for non-isomorphic indecomposables under $\mathrm S$; character calculations give that $B^\uparrow B_s$ is perverse and that $B^\downarrow B_s\cong B^\downarrow(-1)\oplus B^\downarrow(1)$.

**The shifted descent piece does not contribute.** In the decomposition $B^\downarrow B_s\cong B^\downarrow(1)\oplus B^\downarrow(-1)$ the restriction of the Lefschetz form to $B^\downarrow(1)$ is identically zero: left multiplication by $\rho$ satisfies hL on $B^\downarrow$ (the induction hypothesis gives hL on ${}^jF_y(-j)$, and its unshifted block projectors commute with $\rho$, so each descent block inherits hL), so [F5] applies to the shifted piece with $d>0$. Moreover the projection of ${}^jF_x(-j)$ to $B^\downarrow B_s$ lands entirely in $B^\downarrow(1)$: ${}^jF_x(-j)$ lives in perverse degree $0$ by the linearity theorem, and Hom-vanishing between perverse degrees $0$ and $-1$ forces the projection to the $B^\downarrow(-1)$-part to vanish. Hence the image of ${}^jF_x(-j)$ in $B^\downarrow B_s$ contributes nothing to the Lefschetz form.

**All Lefschetz forms and a genuine split inclusion.** The projection onto the surviving factors defines a degree-zero $\rho$-equivariant map $\jmath:{}^jF_x(-j)\to B^\uparrow B_s\oplus{}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$. For every $k\ge0$ and $b,b'$ in source degree $-k$, step 4.1 gives
$\langle b,\rho^kb'\rangle=\langle\jmath(b),\rho^k\jmath(b')\rangle$,
since the omitted shifted-descent factor contributes zero to that Lefschetz form. This is equality of all negative-degree Lefschetz forms, not a degree-one form identity. Applying $q$ to the original split inclusion yields a split inclusion; every map from its perverse source to $B^\downarrow(1)$ vanishes after $q$, since none of those differently shifted indecomposable classes are isomorphic. Hence $q(\jmath)$ is split injective. Lift a left inverse to a morphism $h$ of bimodules. Then $q(h\jmath)=1$, so reflection of isomorphisms by the radical quotient makes $h\jmath$ invertible. The map $(h\jmath)^{-1}h$ is a genuine bimodule left inverse of $\jmath$. Thus $\jmath$ is a split inclusion already before reduction and remains injective after reduction.

**The codomain satisfies the relations with the global sign.** The two orthogonal summands of the codomain are handled as follows. The summand ${}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$ satisfies HR with the global sign of the induction hypothesis for $y$ and $j-1$, namely positivity on primitive degrees congruent to $-\ell(y)+(j-1)=-m+1+j-1=-m+j\pmod4$, which is the required global sign for $x,j$. The summand $B^\uparrow B_s$ satisfies HR by the tensoring lemma [F3]: $B^\uparrow$ is a self-dual direct sum of normalized $B_z$ with $zs>z$, each satisfying $\mathrm{HR}(z,s)$ by hypothesis and hence hL and HR with the standard sign; its restricted form satisfies HR with the inherited global sign by the induction hypothesis and the stable-subspace lemma. Multiply this form by its global factor $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$ to give the standard sign, apply [F3], and undo that same factor on the induced tensor form. The tensor thus has the inherited global sign shifted by one, i.e. positivity on degrees congruent to $(-\ell(y)+j)-1=-m+j\pmod4$. Since the two summands are orthogonal and carry the same global sign, the codomain satisfies HR with the global sign fixed by $-m+j$.

**Inheritance from the negative-degree form identities.** The reduced map $\jmath$ is an injective $\rho$-equivariant graded map into the HR space of step 6.1. Its source has symmetric dimensions by [F2] and normalized self-duality, so ambient hL makes every $\rho^k$ on source degree $-k$ injective, hence an isomorphism onto the opposite degree. Source primitives map into ambient primitives. The identity for every $k$ in step 5.1 therefore makes each source primitive form definite with the required ambient sign. Primitive decomposition on the source now gives nonsingular Lefschetz forms in every negative degree; together with hL and graded symmetry this also proves that its original restricted invariant form is non-degenerate. Thus it satisfies HR. The embedding was chosen before the positive rescalings: the induction gives the properties for every tuple on $F_y$, the orthogonal label blocks are independent of these scalars, and the split projection argument is categorical. Applying this argument for every tuple proves the full simultaneous rescaling assertion and closes the induction.

boundaries.evidence: The empty word is the base of the induction in step 1.1: the complex is the unit concentrated in degree zero, its single summand satisfies the relations trivially, and the existence of the embedding as a direct summand is the identity statement.

The degree-zero summand is the top term of the induction: step 2.1 keeps it as the induction hypothesis for the shorter element, and step 4.1 shows the shifted descent piece contributes nothing to the surviving target.

Unit multiplicity is tracked explicitly: step 3.1 decomposes the fixed degree piece into multiplicity spaces attached to the summands, and step 6.1 handles the single top summand separately from the lower ones.

Degenerate summands are isolated rather than assumed absent: step 4.1 identifies the shifted descent piece whose Lefschetz form vanishes identically and shows it is orthogonal to the surviving summands, so the defect cannot propagate.
The lowest degree of each piece is the anchor of the statement: the conventions fix the bottom degree, and steps 2.1 and 5.1 verify the isometry and the signs beginning at that degree.
Choice-free: the tuples of positive rescaling factors are fixed data of the statement, and the induction of steps 2.1 through 7.1 ranges over finitely many summands.

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts existence of an embedding satisfying a list of positivity conditions; it contains no biconditional and thus no forward direction.
No converse obligation arises: the statement does not claim that the Hodge-Riemann signs characterize the minimal complex.

(1) The quotient $\mathcal B^{ss}$ is semisimple with simple classes $B_x(k)$ and endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$, and $q$ reflects isomorphisms.

(2) Every bounded complex of $\mathcal B$ has a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, and any two minimal models are isomorphic as complexes.

(3) Every direct summand of a perverse (respectively p-split) bimodule is perverse (respectively p-split).

(4) For perverse $M,N$ one has $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N(-i))=0$ for $i>0$.

(5) The perverse cuts on p-split bimodules are independent of the chosen decomposition and are preserved by every morphism.

(6) The definitions of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ can equivalently be tested on the minimal model, and both classes are closed under extensions in distinguished triangles.

**The category and its radical.** Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ be the real
graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad \tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad \tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside
which the Rouquier complexes of the next items are shown to lie, following the
orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.

derivations.claim: **Case (1), positive parameter.** Assume $xs<x$, $\mathrm S(x)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(x)$. By [F1] the reduced operator is the matrix with diagonal blocks $\rho\cdot(-)$ on $B_x(1)$ and $B_x(-1)$ and lower off-diagonal block $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$, a scalar multiple of the identity; since $\rho\cdot(-)$ satisfies hL on $B_x$, the $\rho$-action completes to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb R)$-action and, after rescaling by $\zeta\ne0$, the matrix describes the action of the raising operator on the tensor product of $B_x$ with the two-dimensional standard representation; hence its powers are isomorphisms in the centered degrees and $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds, which is case (1).

**Case (2), setting and form identity.** Assume $\zeta>0$, $xs>x$, $\mathrm S(\le x)$, $\mathrm{HR}(z,t)$ for all $z<x$ with $zt>z$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(<x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x)$. By [F2] the scalars $\gamma_i$ for $1\le i\le m$ are strictly positive and $\gamma_{m+1}=(x^{-1}\rho)(\alpha_s^\vee)+\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$, and with $\varphi:M\to{}^1F_xB_s\oplus B_x(1)$ the first differential of $F_xF_s$ one has $\langle b,L_\zeta b'\rangle_{\overline M}=\langle\overline\varphi(b),\overline\varphi(b')\rangle_\gamma$ for all $b,b'\in\overline M$; by [F3] the reduced $\varphi$ is injective in internal degrees $\le\ell(x)$.

**Failure at $\zeta=0$ for a descent.** At $\zeta=0$ the matrix of [F1] is diagonal with both diagonal blocks the Lefschetz operator of $B_x$; the bottom class $b$ of $B_x(1)$ lies in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and satisfies $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}b=0$, so the centered Lefschetz map of degree $-\ell(x)-1$ fails to be injective; the opposite total degree $+\ell(x)+1$ is nonzero by self-duality of $B_xB_s$, so the failure is genuine and not a vanishing of both sides. This is the failure statement of the theorem.

**The operator commutes with $\varphi$.** Writing $\varphi=(d_1,d_2)$ with $d_1$ into ${}^1F_xB_s$ and $d_2$ into $B_x(1)$, the deleted-word factorization of [F2] shows that $d_1$ commutes with $L_\zeta$ and that $d_2(L_\zeta b)=\rho\cdot d_2(b)+d_2(b)\cdot\zeta\rho$. After right reduction the last right multiple vanishes. Thus, with $L$ equal to $L_\zeta$ on the reduced first summand and $\rho\cdot(-)$ on the reduced second summand, $\overline\varphi(L_\zeta b)=L\overline\varphi(b)$ for every $b\in\overline M$. No such equality with this $L$ is asserted on unreduced $M$.

**The target satisfies HR.** Consider the graded space $W:=\overline{{}^1F_x(-1)B_s}\oplus\overline{B_x}$ with the operator $L$ of step 2.2 and the form $\langle-,-\rangle_\gamma$. The two summands are orthogonal for the induced form, $B_x$ satisfies hL and HR by $\mathrm{HR}(x)$, and ${}^1F_x(-1)B_s$ satisfies hL and HR with the standard sign: its summands $B_z$ with $z<x$ satisfy $\mathrm S(z)$ and, for every such $z$, the hypothesis $\mathrm{HR}(z,s)_\zeta$ (which $\mathrm{HRbar}(<x,s)_\zeta$ supplies, including descents since $\zeta>0$), so the tensoring lemma [F6] applies to ${}^1F_x(-1)=\bigoplus_{z<x}B_z$ with the positivity of the rescalings; the induced signs of ${}^1F_x(-1)$ furnished by [F5] match the standard sign. Hence $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign, and the reduced map $\overline\varphi$ sends $\overline M$ into $W(1)$, since right reduction of the first differential target is $\overline{{}^1F_xB_s}\oplus\overline{B_x}(1)=W(1)$.

**Case (2) concluded.** Apply the weak-Lefschetz substitute [F4] to $\overline\varphi:\overline M\to W(1)$: its three hypotheses hold by steps 1.2, 2.2 and 3.1 (injectivity in degrees $\le\ell(x)$ contains injectivity in degrees $\le-1$, the form identity is the one of [F2], and $W$ satisfies HR by step 3.1). Hence $L_\zeta^k:\overline M^{-k}\to\overline M^k$ is injective for all $k\ge0$; since $\overline M$ has symmetric dimensions by self-duality, equal dimensions give isomorphisms, which is $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ and proves case (2).

Use the same positive scalars $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_{m+1}$ with $\zeta=0$ and the same form identity as in [F2] with $\varphi$ the first differential of $F_xF_s$. Decompose ${}^1F_x(-1)=B^\uparrow\oplus B^\downarrow$ orthogonally according to $zs>z$ and $zs<z$ as in step 3.1; by [F7] the complex $F_xF_s$ lies in $pK^b_{\ge0}$. boundaries.reason: The theorem fixes the ascent or descent pair and the bimodule built from it; the three listed cases are exhaustive and the statement contains no empty family or empty summation needing interpretation.

boundaries.evidence: The zero parameter is an entire case of the theorem: step 2.1 exhibits the failure at vanishing parameter in the descent situation, while steps 4.2 and 5.1 prove the ascent case there by separating the kernel of the third differential component.
The multiplicity-one summands B_x(1) and B_x(-1) of the descent decomposition, and the single top summand B_x of the target constructed in step 3.1, are the unit-multiplicity pieces the proof tracks.

The degenerate zero-parameter descent case is genuinely excluded from hard Lefschetz and is displayed as the failure clause of step 2.1, while the positive-parameter descent case is recovered in step 1.1 by an explicit rescaling.
The parameter endpoints are separated by the case list, and the grading endpoints enter through steps 2.1 and 5.1, which evaluate the bottom class and its powers up to the extreme degree.
Choice-free: the complexes and forms are fixed by the suppliers, and the only rescaling in step 1.1 is by the explicit positive real parameter.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is a three-case implication list together with a failure statement; it asserts no equivalence, so there is no forward direction to discharge.
No converse is claimed: the hypotheses are sufficient conditions for hard Lefschetz in each case, not a characterization.
