citations.quote:
**The parabolic.** Keep $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$, the
simple reflections $s_i=(i\ i+1)$ and the invariants $R^{s_i}$ of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]], and let
$1\le i\le n-2$. Put
$$W_{i,i+1}:=\langle s_i,s_{i+1}\rangle\le S_n,\qquad R^{W_{i,i+1}}:=R^{s_i}\cap R^{s_{i+1}},$$
the parabolic subgroup generated by the two adjacent simple reflections and its
invariant ring. The two generators act as adjacent transpositions on the three indicated
coordinates and fix every other coordinate, so their restriction is an
isomorphism $W_{i,i+1}\cong S_3$ by the generation clause of
[[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]]; the subgroup permutes the three coordinates
$x_i,x_{i+1},x_{i+2}$ and fixes every other coordinate, so $R^{W_{i,i+1}}$ is
the ring of polynomials in $x_i,x_{i+1},x_{i+2}$ that are invariant under all
permutations of the three, with all other $x_j$ adjoined as invariants. The
element
$$w_{i,i+1}:=s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}\in W_{i,i+1}$$
is the longest element of $W_{i,i+1}$, of length $3$.

**The bimodule.** Define
$$B_{i,i+1,i}:=R\otimes_{R^{W_{i,i+1}}}R(3),$$
the balanced tensor product of the $(R,R^{W_{i,i+1}})$-bimodule $R$ with the
$(R^{W_{i,i+1}},R)$-bimodule $R$, with the total grading of the tensor product
shifted by the external shift $(3)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]], that is
$$(3)=\{-3\},\qquad (B_{i,i+1,i})_d=\bigl(R\otimes_{R^{W_{i,i+1}}}R\bigr)_{d+3} \ \ \text{in the convention } M(r)_d=M_{d+r}.$$
It is the *rank-two longest type-A Soergel bimodule* attached to $i$. Equivalently
$B_{i,i+1,i}=R\otimes_{R^{W_{i,i+1}}}R\{-3\}$ in the internal notation
$M\{r\}_d=M_{d-r}$ of the library, and when $n=3$ and $i=1$ it is
$B_{1,2,1}=R\otimes_{R^{S_3}}R(3)$. The Bott–Samelson bimodule of the word
$(i,i+1,i)$ is
$$B_{\underline{i,i+1,i}}=B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i =R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R\otimes_{R^{s_{i+1}}}R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(3)$$
in the notation of [[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]].

**The reduction.** Work over the ring $S=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of the real
scalar-extension definition ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]),
with $S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$ the ideal of positive-degree elements; the residue
field of the right action is
$$k:=S/S_+=\mathbb R,$$
with quotient map $S\twoheadrightarrow k$, $s\mapsto \bar s$. For a graded
$(S,S)$-bimodule $M$ that is finite free as a right $S$-module put
$$\overline M:=M\otimes_Sk=M/MS_+,$$
the **reduction** of $M$: a finite-dimensional graded $k$-vector space, on which
the left $S$-action descends because $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $MS_+$ is
stable under left multiplication. Write $\overline M^{\,i}$ for its homogeneous
component of degree $i$, $d_i(M):=\dim_{\mathbb R}\overline M^{\,i}$ for the
graded dimensions, and
$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Indeed, $(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)=c_{w^{-1}(i)}-c_{w^{-1}(i+1)}$ is positive
exactly when $w^{-1}(i)<w^{-1}(i+1)$, the left-ascent criterion for inversion
length. Thus the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The reduced module $\overline{B_x^R}$ has bottom degree
$-\ell(x)$ and top degree $+\ell(x)$; the unreduced bimodule has nonzero
components in arbitrarily high degrees. On a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; in particular every $\underline H_w$ has integer nonnegative coefficients in the standard basis with $p_{y,w}$ of fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

Let $n\ge2$ and $k=\mathbb Q$, let $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ be
the split Grothendieck ring of the type-A Soergel category
([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]) and let
$h_\Delta,h_\nabla$ be the intrinsic $\Delta$- and $\nabla$-multiplicity
characters of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]],
which by [[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] are
well-defined functions of the bimodule and additive on direct sums, so that
they descend to $\mathbb Z$-linear maps on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$
with values in the Hecke algebra $H_{S_n}$ of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] whose normalized
generators are $H_i=v(T_i+1)$. Then:

1. $h_\Delta$ is a homomorphism of $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebras
   $$h_\Delta:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad h_\Delta(XY)=h_\Delta(X)h_\Delta(Y),\qquad h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X),$$ that is
   $h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X)$, and $h_\Delta([B_i])=H_i$ for every simple
   reflection;
2. $h_\nabla$ is multiplicative, $h_\nabla(XY)=h_\nabla(X)h_\nabla(Y)$, and
   semilinear for the involution $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ of the coefficients:
   $h_\nabla(vX)=v^{-1}h_\nabla(X)$ and $h_\nabla([B_i])=H_i$; equivalently
   $h_\nabla=d\circ h_\Delta$, where $d$ is the semilinear algebra involution
   of $H_{S_n}$ determined by $d(v)=v^{-1}$ and $d(T_i)=T_i^{-1}$;
3. for every Bott–Samelson word $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ one has
   $h_\Delta(B_{\underline i})=h_\nabla(B_{\underline i})=H_{i_1}\cdots H_{i_r}$,
   and for every bimodule $M$ in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$ and simple reflection
   $s_i$ the simple-generator recursion
   $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$,
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$ holds; in the Elias–Williamson
   grading shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$
   and $h_\nabla$ by $v^{-1}$.

Let $1\le i\le n-2$, put $s:=s_i$, $t:=s_{i+1}$ and write
$B_iB_{i+1}B_i:=B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i$. Then there are degree-zero
isomorphisms of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_i,\qquad B_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_{i+1},$$
with no additional grading shift on any summand, where $B_{i,i+1,i}$ is the
rank-two longest bimodule of
[[def-the-rank-two-longest-type-a-soergel-bimodule]]. On split Grothendieck
classes the two decompositions read $[B_iB_{i+1}B_i]=[B_{i,i+1,i}]+[B_i]$ and
$[B_{i+1}B_iB_{i+1}]=[B_{i,i+1,i}]+[B_{i+1}]$.

derivations.claim: **The bimodule and its reduction.** Symmetric polynomials in three variables are generated by $e_1,e_2,e_3$: for a homogeneous symmetric polynomial, its lexicographically leading monomial has exponents $a\ge b\ge c$; subtracting its coefficient times $e_1^{a-b}e_2^{b-c}e_3^c$ lowers that leading monomial. The finite set of monomials of the fixed total degree makes this reduction terminate. Thus $S^{S_3}=\mathbb R[e_1,e_2,e_3]$ and [F1] gives the reduced module $C(3)$ with $C=S/(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Eliminating $x_3=-x-y$ gives $C=\mathbb R[x,y]/(x^3,y^2+xy+x^2)$: the $e_3$ relation is $x^2y+xy^2=0$, and subtracting this from $x(x^2+xy+y^2)=0$ gives $x^3=0$, with the same identities proving the reverse inclusion of ideals. Over $\mathbb R[x]/(x^3)$, division by the monic quadratic in $y$ gives the free basis $1,y$; hence $1,x,y,x^2,xy,x^2y$ is a real basis and the dimensions are $1,2,2,1$ in degrees $0,2,4,6$, centered at $-3,-1,1,3$ after shifting by $(3)$. The tensor bimodule is generated as a bimodule by $1\otimes1$ and its bottom component is one dimensional, so every degree-zero endomorphism is scalar; it is therefore indecomposable. The balanced surjection $f\otimes g\mapsto f w_0(g)$ onto $S_{w_0}$ proves that it has the $w_0$ graph in its support. In the rank-two decomposition it is the summand carrying the $w_0$ graph (the other summand $B_{s_1}$ has only the $e,s_1$ graphs), so its label is $w_0$.

**The Kazhdan-Lusztig element.** Put $A:=v-v^{-1}$ and $J:=H_{w_0}+v(H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1})+v^2(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+v^3$. The element $J$ lies in $H_{w_0}+\sum_{y<w_0}v\mathbb Z[v]H_y$, since all coefficients belong to $v\mathbb Z[v]$. For bar-invariance we expand: from $H_s^{-1}=H_s+A$ and the reduced products $H_{s_1}H_{s_2}=H_{s_1s_2}$ and $H_{s_1s_2}H_{s_1}=H_{w_0}$ one computes $\overline{H_{s_1s_2}}=H_{s_1s_2}+A(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+A^2$ and $\overline{H_{w_0}}=H_{w_0}+A(H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1})+A^2(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+A+A^3$, while $\overline{H_{s_1}}=H_{s_1}+A$ and $\overline{H_{s_2}}=H_{s_2}+A$. Applying the semilinear involution to $J$ gives $\overline J=\overline{H_{w_0}}+v^{-1}(\overline{H_{s_1s_2}}+\overline{H_{s_2s_1}})+v^{-2}(\overline{H_{s_1}}+\overline{H_{s_2}})+v^{-3}$; collecting coefficients in the standard basis, the coefficient of $H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1}$ becomes $A+v^{-1}=v$, the coefficient of $H_{s_1}+H_{s_2}$ becomes $A^2+2v^{-1}A+v^{-2}=v^2$, and the coefficient of $H_e$ becomes $A+A^3+2v^{-1}A^2+2v^{-2}A+v^{-3}=v^3$. Hence $\overline J=J$, and by the uniqueness clause of [F2] $J=\underline H_{w_0}$.

**Character and multiplicities.** By [F4], $\operatorname{ch}(B_{w_0})=(H_{s_1}+v)(H_{s_2}+v)(H_{s_1}+v)-(H_{s_1}+v)=J$, the last equality following by the quadratic relation $H_s^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_s$ and reduced multiplication. Step 1.2 gives $J=\underline H_{w_0}$, so the $\Delta$-multiplicities of $B_{w_0}$ are exactly the six coefficients of $J$, one for each of the six elements of $S_3$. Reading them through [F3], the layer $\Delta_{w_0}(0)$ contributes in degree $\ell(w_0)=3$, the two layers $\Delta_{s_1s_2}(1),\Delta_{s_2s_1}(1)$ contribute in degree $1$ with multiplicity two, the two layers $\Delta_{s_1}(2),\Delta_{s_2}(2)$ contribute in degree $-1$ with multiplicity two and the layer $\Delta_e(3)$ contributes in degree $-3$; this is the graded dimension $1,2,2,1$ of the centered coinvariant algebra computed in step 1.1, and the value at $v=1$ is $6=\dim C$. The coefficients $P_{e,w_0}=P_{s_i,w_0}=P_{s_1s_2,w_0}=P_{s_2s_1,w_0}=1$ are the classical normalization of these coefficients. This verifies the example.

   grading shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$
   and $h_\nabla$ by $v^{-1}$.

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; in particular every $\underline H_w$ has integer nonnegative coefficients in the standard basis with $p_{y,w}$ of fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

Let $1\le i\le n-2$, put $s:=s_i$, $t:=s_{i+1}$ and write
$B_iB_{i+1}B_i:=B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i$. Then there are degree-zero
isomorphisms of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$B_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_i,\qquad B_{i+1}\otimes_RB_i\otimes_RB_{i+1}\cong B_{i,i+1,i}\oplus B_{i+1},$$
with no additional grading shift on any summand, where $B_{i,i+1,i}$ is the
rank-two longest bimodule of
[[def-the-rank-two-longest-type-a-soergel-bimodule]]. On split Grothendieck
classes the two decompositions read $[B_iB_{i+1}B_i]=[B_{i,i+1,i}]+[B_i]$ and
$[B_{i+1}B_iB_{i+1}]=[B_{i,i+1,i}]+[B_{i+1}]$.

**Scalar extension of the published realization.** The published type-A page
works over $k=\mathbb Q$ with the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
and the two normalizations of the simple roots of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]: the coordinate roots
$\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$ and the alternating balanced roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}=\varepsilon_i\beta_i$, $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$. For
the Hodge-theoretic statements of this page we extend scalars along
$\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ and set
$$S:=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\qquad \deg x_i=2,$$
with $S_0=\mathbb R$ and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces $S_d$; the
symmetric group $S_n$ acts by the place permutations
$w\cdot x_i:=x_{w(i)}$ ([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]).
On this page $\alpha_i$ always means the coordinate root
$\alpha_i:=\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$, and $\alpha_i^\vee:=\beta_i^\vee$ is the
coordinate coroot, so that under the standard form the Cartan entries are
$\langle\alpha_i^\vee,\alpha_j\rangle=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{|i-j|,1}$ and
adjacent entries are $-1$; the reflection is
$s_i(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha_i\rangle\alpha_i^\vee$. The alternating balanced
roots $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}$ are retained by the published page for its
diagrammatic presentation and are not used for positivity, Demazure traces or
descent signs on this page; both choices define the same reflections, the same
reflecting hyperplanes, the same invariant rings $S^{s_i}$ and the same
underlying bimodules, and they differ only by the unit $\pm1$ in front of the
root, which changes no tensor bimodule but does change the normalization of
$\partial_i$ and of the trace.

**The real generators and the real category.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ set
$$B_i^R:=S\otimes_{S^{s_i}}S(1),$$
the balanced tensor product of the $(S,S^{s_i})$-bimodule $S$ with the
$(S^{s_i},S)$-bimodule $S$, shifted in the Elias-Williamson convention
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$ used on this page ([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]],
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Its left basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ have degrees $-1$ and $+1$, and
$B_i^R$ is finite free of rank two on each side
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]). The **real
type-A Soergel category** $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ is the idempotent completion
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) of the full subcategory of graded
$(S,S)$-bimodules whose objects are the finite direct sums of shifts
$B_{\underline i}^R(d)=B_{i_1}^R\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{i_r}^R(d)$ of real
Bott-Samelson products ([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with the
same internal shifts as the rational category, i.e. $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$ in the
Elias-Williamson convention. Its unit is the graded ring $S$ itself, regarded
as an object in cohomological degree zero; it is not a polynomial ring
concentrated in internal degree zero. Categorically,
$\mathrm{SBim}_n^R=\mathrm{Kar}(\mathrm{BSBim}_n^R)$ has the same formal
properties as the rational Soergel category: it is graded, additive,
idempotent-complete and monoidal with unit $S$, and every object is a finite
direct sum of graded shifts of indecomposables.

**Scalar extension of objects.** For a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ over the
rational polynomial ring put $M^R:=M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, with the
$S$-actions induced from the $R$-actions and the tensor grading. Since
$\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R$ is flat, scalar extension is exact on graded pieces;
it carries the rational generator $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ to $B_i^R$, the
rational Bott-Samelson construction to the real one, and the rational
idempotent completion to the real one. Standard graph supports, the
$\Delta$- and $\nabla$-flags with their characters, and all formulas of the
rational page are read over $\mathbb R$ after extension. The Hecke algebra
used for characters is the integral normalized algebra
$H_v(n)$ over $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with basis $H_x$ of
[[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]; it is the same
algebra before and after the scalar extension, since it is defined over
$\mathbb Z$.

**The dominant chamber.** The **dominant chamber** on this page is the set of
strictly dominant degree-two elements
$$\Theta:=\Bigl\{\rho=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j\ :\ c_j\in\mathbb R,\ c_j>c_{j+1}\ \text{for } 1\le j\le n-1\Bigr\}\subset S_2 .$$
It is nonempty, for example for $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$, which gives
$c_j-c_{j+1}=1$ for every $j$. For $\rho=\sum_jc_jx_j$ the coordinate
evaluation is $\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)=\rho(x_i-x_{i+1})=c_i-c_{i+1}$, so
$\rho\in\Theta$ is exactly a degree-two element with
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot; no alternating-sign chamber
and no replacement of $\rho$ is used anywhere on this page.

**Conventions.** All tensor products are over $S$ unless indicated, all shifts
are the internal shifts just fixed, "form" on this page always means a graded
symmetric form that is $S$-bilinear for the right action and invariant under
the left action in the sense fixed by the intersection-form definition below, and
dimensions of reduced modules are always real dimensions. The rational
comparison statements needed for labels, characters and forms are collected
in the comparison lemma later on this page.

derivations.claim: **The character of the two-letter product.** By [F1] and multiplicativity, $\operatorname{ch}(B_sB_t)=(H_s+v)(H_t+v)=H_sH_t+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$; since $st$ is reduced, [F2] gives $H_sH_t=H_{st}$, so the standard-basis expansion is $H_{st}+vH_s+vH_t+v^2$. Its coefficients give the multiplicities $1,1,1,1$ displayed, and reading the layers through [F1] the reduced dimension is $1+1+1+1=4$.

**The Kazhdan-Lusztig element of $st$.** Put $A:=v-v^{-1}$ and $J:=H_{st}+v(H_s+H_t)+v^2$; then $J\in H_{st}+v\mathbb Z[v]H_s+v\mathbb Z[v]H_t+v^2\mathbb Z[v]$. Since $H_s^{-1}=H_s+A$, $H_t^{-1}=H_t+A$ and $\overline{H_{st}}=H_{ts}^{-1}=H_s^{-1}H_t^{-1}=(H_s+A)(H_t+A)=H_{st}+A(H_s+H_t)+A^2$ (the last identity uses $H_sH_t=H_{st}$), applying the semilinear involution gives $\overline J=\overline{H_{st}}+v^{-1}(\overline{H_s}+\overline{H_t})+v^{-2}=H_{st}+A(H_s+H_t)+A^2+v^{-1}(H_s+H_t)+2v^{-1}A+v^{-2}$, whose coefficients are $A+v^{-1}=v$ at $H_s+H_t$ and $A^2+2v^{-1}A+v^{-2}=(v^2-2+v^{-2})+(2-2v^{-2})+v^{-2}=v^2$ at $H_e$; hence $\overline J=J$, and by uniqueness [F2], $J=\underline H_{st}$.

**Indecomposability of $B_sB_t$.** The unshifted tensor $M=S\otimes_{S^s}S\otimes_{S^t}S$ is generated as a bimodule by $1\otimes1\otimes1$. To see this, write a middle polynomial as $h_0+x_1h_1$ with $h_0,h_1\in S^s$, which slide to the first slot. The remaining $x_1$ slides to the last slot because $t=s_2$ fixes $x_1$. Therefore every tensor is a sum of $p(1\otimes1\otimes1)q$. After the shift $(2)$ its lowest component is one-dimensional in degree $-2$, by its finite left tensor basis and $S_0=\mathbb R$. A degree-zero bimodule endomorphism must send the generator to a scalar multiple of itself, and generation forces that same scalar on all of $M$. Hence its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, with no nontrivial idempotent, so $B_sB_t$ is indecomposable. The balanced map $p\otimes q\otimes r\mapsto p\,s(q)\,st(r)$ is surjective onto the $st$ graph bimodule, showing that this indecomposable has the top graph of its reduced word; it is the normalized summand $B_{st}$. Thus $B_sB_t\cong B_{st}$ with no lower summands, independently of the Hom formula.

**The three-letter braid relation.** By multiplicativity and the products computed in steps 1.1 and 2.1, $\operatorname{ch}(B_sB_tB_s)=\underline H_s\underline H_t\underline H_s=\underline H_{st}\underline H_s$; expanding with the Hecke relations gives $\underline H_{st}\underline H_s=\underline H_{sts}+\underline H_s$ Indeed the expansion is $J_0+H_s+v$ where $J_0=H_{sts}+v(H_{st}+H_{ts})+v^2(H_s+H_t)+v^3$. The element $J_0=\underline H_{st}\underline H_s-\underline H_s$ is bar fixed, with triangular lower coefficients in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, so uniqueness in [F2] identifies it with $\underline H_{sts}$. The reduced dimensions add to $6+2=8$. Exchanging $s$ and $t$ in [F3] gives $B_tB_sB_t\cong B_{sts}\oplus B_t$, whose character differs by $\underline H_t-\underline H_s=H_t-H_s\ne0$, so these Bott-Samelson products are not isomorphic; the rank-two Kazhdan-Lusztig data $P_{e,st}=P_{s,st}=P_{t,st}=1$ are the coefficients displayed in step 2.1. This verifies the example.

Take $n=3$ and let $w_0=s_1s_2s_1$ be the longest element of $S_3$. Then $B_{w_0}=S\otimes_{S^{S_3}}S(3)$ and its reduced module is $C(3)$, where $C=S/(S^{S_3}_+)$ is the unshifted coinvariant algebra: $C$ has the Poincare polynomial $1+2t^2+2t^4+t^6$, so $\dim C=6$, and in the centered grading
$$\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{-3}=\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{3}=1,\qquad \dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{1}=2 .$$
The standard-basis expansion of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element is
$$\underline H_{w_0}=H_{w_0}+v(H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1})+v^2(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+v^3,$$
obtained by solving the bar-invariance and triangularity conditions with coefficients in $v^d\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; its coefficients are non-negative, its value at $v=1$ sums to $6=\dim C$, and it agrees with the rank-one and rank-two Kazhdan-Lusztig data $P_{e,w_0}=P_{s_i,w_0}=P_{w,w_0}=1$ for $\ell(w)=2$. Hence $\operatorname{ch}(B_{w_0})=\underline H_{w_0}$: Soergel's conjecture holds for the longest element of $S_3$, and the $\Delta$-multiplicities of the coinvariant bimodule are the six coefficients just displayed, one for each element of $S_3$.

**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=\underline H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form when $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here $d=\ell(x)$ by the proved normalized degree bounds. The property $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ always denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on $\overline{B_x^R}$, independently of $\mathrm{S}(x)$. $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the conjunction of $\mathrm{S}(x)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations with the standard sign for this normalized intrinsic form; its existence and uniqueness, and the nonzero positive bottom value used for normalization, are proved in [[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires the general Hodge-Riemann relations above for the restricted intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.

Take $n=3$ and let $w_0=s_1s_2s_1$ be the longest element of $S_3$. Then $B_{w_0}=S\otimes_{S^{S_3}}S(3)$ and its reduced module is $C(3)$, where $C=S/(S^{S_3}_+)$ is the unshifted coinvariant algebra: $C$ has the Poincare polynomial $1+2t^2+2t^4+t^6$, so $\dim C=6$, and in the centered grading
$$\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{-3}=\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{3}=1,\qquad \dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{-1}=\dim(\overline{B_{w_0}})^{1}=2 .$$
The standard-basis expansion of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element is
$$\underline H_{w_0}=H_{w_0}+v(H_{s_1s_2}+H_{s_2s_1})+v^2(H_{s_1}+H_{s_2})+v^3,$$
obtained by solving the bar-invariance and triangularity conditions with coefficients in $v^d\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; its coefficients are non-negative, its value at $v=1$ sums to $6=\dim C$, and it agrees with the rank-one and rank-two Kazhdan-Lusztig data $P_{e,w_0}=P_{s_i,w_0}=P_{w,w_0}=1$ for $\ell(w)=2$. Hence $\operatorname{ch}(B_{w_0})=\underline H_{w_0}$: Soergel's conjecture holds for the longest element of $S_3$, and the $\Delta$-multiplicities of the coinvariant bimodule are the six coefficients just displayed, one for each element of $S_3$.

derivations.claim: **The two-variable model.** Put $x=x_1$, $y=x_2$ and $x_3=-x-y$. Then $e_1=x+y+x_3=0$, while $e_2=x_1x_2+x_1x_3+x_2x_3=xy+x(-x-y)+y(-x-y)=-(x^2+xy+y^2)$ and $e_3=x_1x_2x_3=-x^2y-xy^2$; hence the coinvariant ideal is generated by $x^2+xy+y^2$ and $x^2y+xy^2$, and since $x^3=x(x^2+xy+y^2)-x^2y-xy^2$ the second relation can be replaced by $x^3=0$, giving $C=\mathbb R[x,y]/(x^2+xy+y^2,x^3)$. The monomials $1;x,y;x^2,xy;x^2y$ span it: the relations $x^2=-xy-y^2$ and $x^3=0$, together with $xy^2=-x^2y$ and $y^3=0$, reduce every monomial of degree $\ge 2$ in $x$ to one of them, and their independence follows by monic division by $y^2+xy+x^2$ over $\mathbb R[x]/(x^3)$, which gives the free basis $1,y$ over that ring.

**The trace and pairing.** The rank-two summand map $j(p\otimes q)=p\otimes1\otimes1\otimes q$ pulls the Bott–Samelson trace back to $\partial_1\partial_2\partial_1(p)q$, as follows by taking the right-coefficient trace successively in the three slots; this is the explicit trace calculation in the rank-two decomposition proof, also obtained directly from the rank-one trace convention. After right reduction it is the top trace on $C$, since $\partial_1(x_1^2x_2)=x_1x_2$, $\partial_2(x_1x_2)=x_1$ and $\partial_1(x_1)=1$. Hence $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$ and all degrees other than $6$ have zero trace. The complementary-degree pairings are $1$ in degrees $0,6$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ in degrees $2,4$, of determinant $-1$; they prove nondegeneracy directly. The form used below is therefore the actual induced reduced intersection form, without invoking the general Hodge theorem.

**The special dominant element.** For $\rho=2x+y$ one computes $\rho x=2x^2+xy$ and $\rho y=2xy+y^2=-x^2+xy$ using $y^2=-x^2-xy$; the matrix of $\rho$ from the degree-$2$ block with basis $(x,y)$ to the degree-$4$ block with basis $(x^2,xy)$ is therefore $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is $3\ne0$, so $\rho:C^{-1}\to C^{1}$ is an isomorphism. Moreover $\rho^2x=3x^2y$ and $\rho^2y=0$: indeed $x^2\rho=x^2(2x+y)=2x^3+x^2y=x^2y$, $xy\rho=xy(2x+y)=2x^2y+xy^2=x^2y$; hence $\rho^2x=2\cdot x^2y+x^2y=3x^2y$ and $\rho^2y=-x^2y+x^2y=0$; hence $P^{-1}=\ker(\rho^2)=\mathbb Ry$ and $\rho^3(1)=\rho^2(2x+y)=6x^2y\ne0$, so $\rho^3:C^{-3}\to C^{3}$ is an isomorphism as both sides are one-dimensional.

**The signs for the special element.** With the normalization $\operatorname{Tr}(x^2y)=1$, the bottom primitive form is $(1,1)=\operatorname{Tr}(1\cdot\rho^3(1))=\operatorname{Tr}(6x^2y)=6>0$, positive as required in degree $-3$; the middle primitive form is $(y,y)=\operatorname{Tr}(y\cdot\rho y)=\operatorname{Tr}(y(-x^2+xy))=\operatorname{Tr}(-x^2y+xy^2)=-1-1=-2<0$, negative as required in degree $-1$, where the standard sign is $(-1)^{(3-1)/2}=-1$. The primitive decomposition is read off from the two strings: $1\mapsto 2x+y\mapsto 3x^2+3xy\mapsto 6x^2y$ spans the four degrees with one vector each, and $y\mapsto -x^2+xy$ spans degrees $-1$ and $+1$; together they account for all four graded pieces and their dimensions, so there are exactly one length-four string and one length-two string.

**The general dominant chamber.** Let $\rho=c_1x_1+c_2x_2+c_3x_3$ be strictly dominant, so $c_1>c_2>c_3$; subtracting a multiple of $e_1$ (which is zero in $C$) writes its class as $\rho=ax+by$ with $a=c_1-c_3>b=c_2-c_3>0$. Then $\rho x=ax^2+bxy$ and $\rho y=-bx^2+(a-b)xy$, so the middle matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a-b\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $D=a^2-ab+b^2>0$, and $\rho^3(1)=3ab(a-b)x^2y$: indeed $\rho^2x=b(2a-b)x^2y$ and $\rho^2y=a(a-2b)x^2y$, so $p:=a(a-2b)x-b(2a-b)y$ satisfies $\rho^2p=0$, and expanding gives $\operatorname{Tr}(p\rho p)=A^2b-B^2a+2AB(b-a)$ with $A=a(a-2b)$, $B=b(2a-b)$, which simplifies to $-3ab(a-b)(a^2-ab+b^2)<0$. Hence $P^{-1}=\mathbb Rp$ (one-dimensional, since $p\ne0$ for $a>b>0$) carries a negative definite Lefschetz form, the bottom form $\operatorname{Tr}(3ab(a-b)x^2y)>0$ is positive, and every strictly dominant $\rho$ satisfies hard Lefschetz with the standard signs on both primitive spaces.

**Conclusion.** Steps 2.1 and 3.1 verify the displayed isomorphisms, the two primitive spaces and their signs for the explicit choice, and step 5.1 shows the same for every strictly dominant element; the primitive decomposition has the two strings claimed. This verifies the example by its quotient and trace calculations.

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$, both of degrees $-1$ and $1$; and every
Bott–Samelson tensor product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite
free as a left $R$-module and finite free as a right $R$-module.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule lying in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that it
carries a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag. Then:

1. the graded multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ of
   [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are
   independent of the compatible enumeration of the flag, so that the character
   sums $h_\Delta(M)$ and $h_\nabla(M)$ are functions of $M$ alone;
2. if $M=M'\oplus M''$ with $M',M''\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, then
   $(M:\Delta_x(d))=(M':\Delta_x(d))+(M'':\Delta_x(d))$ and likewise for
   $\nabla$; more generally the same holds for any direct summand $N$ of $M$
   which itself lies in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

Let $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ be a word in simple reflections and
$B_{\underline i}:=B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$, with
$B_\emptyset=R$. Then $B_{\underline i}$ belongs to both $F_\Delta$ and
$F_\nabla$: it has a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag in the sense of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], its
support is contained in $Gr(S_n)$, and each successive quotient of these flags
is a standard bimodule $R_x\{a\}$ with $x$ a product
$x=s_{i_{j_1}}\cdots s_{i_{j_m}}$ ($1\le j_1<\cdots<j_m\le r$) of a
subexpression of $\underline i$ formed by keeping $m$ letters; the Coxeter
length $\ell(x)$ can be smaller than $m$. The shift $a$ of an occurrence
is computed recursively, one step $\pm1$ per letter of $\underline i$, from the
two rank-one exact sequences of step 1.2 below: the $\Delta$-chart and the
$\nabla$-chart use the two different sequences, so the shift depends on the
chosen subexpression and on the chart, and it is *not* a function of the lengths
and descent numbers of the subexpression alone: for the one-letter word $(s)$
the $\nabla$-chart occurrences are $R\{1\}$ and $R_s\{-1\}$, while the
$\Delta$-chart occurrences are the translates $\Delta_e(1)=R\{-1\}$ and
$\Delta_s(0)=R_s\{1\}$ of the same two subexpressions, so the same subexpression
carries different shifts in the two charts. In particular the number of occurrences of a graph $x$ in the
$\Delta$-flag and in the $\nabla$-flag of $B_{\underline i}$ is the number of
subexpressions of $\underline i$ with product $x$. Moreover $B_{\underline i}$
is finite free of rank $2^r$ as a left
$R$-module and as a right $R$-module, and the flag categories are closed under
tensoring with a generator on either side: if $M\in F_\Delta$ then
$B_s\otimes_RM\in F_\Delta$ and $M\otimes_RB_s\in F_\Delta$, and likewise with
$\nabla$ in place of $\Delta$.

derivations.claim: A finite-dimensional endomorphism algebra and the absence of nontrivial idempotents imply locality. Indeed for an endomorphism $f$ its polynomial minimal relation splits into a power of $T$ and a factor coprime to $T$. The polynomial Chinese remainder identity produces an idempotent separating the nilpotent and invertible parts; indecomposability forces one part to vanish. Thus every $f$ is invertible or nilpotent, and a nonunit $f$ has $1-f$ invertible. Nonunits form a two-sided ideal: multiplication cannot make a nonunit invertible in a finite-dimensional algebra; if two nonunits summed to a unit, dividing their sum would express $1$ as two nonunits, contradicting the invertibility of $1-f$. This is the unique maximal ideal. Its powers eventually vanish: if a power stabilizes, take a minimal finite generating list for that stable ideal and express its last generator using coefficients in the maximal ideal; the invertibility of $1-a$ for such a coefficient eliminates that generator, a contradiction.

Split idempotents until indecomposable summands remain. Each split reduces the positive right rank of its summand, so there are only finitely many splits. The resulting summands have local endomorphism rings by step 1.1. Decompositions are unique: in two finite decompositions, express the identity of one indecomposable as the sum of its composites through the summands of the other. The local maximal ideal cannot contain every composite; an invertible composite gives a split inclusion into one indecomposable summand, hence an isomorphism to it. Remove the common summand and repeat. This proves finite Krull-Schmidt existence and uniqueness.

Decompose a reduced word for $x$. Its top layer is a single $\Delta_x$ by [F4], and the top-layer functor is additive by [F2]. Exactly one indecomposable summand therefore has this graph, with precisely this normalized layer; call it $B_x$. All other summands have support strictly below $x$. This constructs a normalized candidate without any character conjecture.

Let $M$ be any nonzero Soergel object and choose a maximal support label $x$. The two graph layers $\Gamma_xM$ and $\Gamma^xM$ are identified by multiplication by $p_x$ as in [F2]. Choose one homogeneous basis element $m$ of the latter, and let $d$ make its degree equal to the generator degree of $\Gamma^xB_x(d)$. Choose graph maps $f_0:\Gamma^xB_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$ taking that generator to $m$, and $g_0:\Gamma_xM\to\Gamma_xB_x(d)$ which takes the corresponding element $p_xm$ to the generator $p_xb$ and kills the other basis elements. These maps are homogeneous of degree zero and satisfy the identity on the rank-one $x$ layer.

Lift these maps to bimodule maps $f:B_x(d)\to M$ and $g:M\to B_x(d)$. The quotient map $M\to\Gamma^xM$ is the last step of a $\nabla$ flag with $x$ last; its kernel is flagged, so [F3] lifts the map $B_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$. The inclusion $\Gamma_xM\to M$ is the first step of a $\Delta$ flag with $x$ first; its quotient is flagged, so [F3] lifts $g_0$ followed by $\Gamma_xB_x(d)\to B_x(d)$. The first lifted map on the quotient and the second on the submodule agree with the prescribed graph maps. The image identity $\Gamma_xM=\Gamma^xM p_x$ makes their composite $gf$ act as the identity on $\Gamma_xB_x(d)$. Thus $gf$ is not nilpotent, and is invertible by step 1.1. Rescale $g$ by its inverse to exhibit $B_x(d)$ as a summand of $M$.

If $M$ is indecomposable, step 5.1 gives $M\cong B_x(d)$. If two normalized candidates were obtained from different reduced expressions for $x$, applying that same splitting argument to either candidate makes them isomorphic, because their normalized rank-one top degrees force $d=0$. Distinct labels cannot be isomorphic, by their maximal support; distinct shifts at a fixed label cannot be isomorphic, by their top generator degrees. This proves classification and reduced-word independence.

Restriction of degree-zero endomorphisms of $B_x$ to its rank-one top layer is a unital homomorphism onto $k$, since homogeneous scalars act there and its endomorphism ring in degree zero is $k$. Its kernel is a maximal ideal. Locality in step 1.1 makes this the unique maximal ideal, so the residue field is $k$. All selections were from finite supports and finite homogeneous bases, and no choice axiom beyond finite choice is used. The statement follows from steps 2.1, 3.1, 6.1 and this residue calculation.

This supplies the split summand, shift uniqueness and residue field without a KL character assumption. Empty word is the unit and the zero object requires no maximal support selection. citations.quote: Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. For every $x\in S_n$ there is a unique normalized indecomposable $B_x$ supported on $\{y:y\le x\}$ with top $\Delta$ layer exactly $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. It is the unique summand with the $x$ graph of any reduced Bott-Samelson word for $x$. Every indecomposable is exactly one $B_x(d)$. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

**Scalar extension of the published realization.** The published type-A page
works over $k=\mathbb Q$ with the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
and the two normalizations of the simple roots of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]: the coordinate roots
$\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$ and the alternating balanced roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}=\varepsilon_i\beta_i$, $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$. For
the Hodge-theoretic statements of this page we extend scalars along
$\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ and set
$$S:=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\qquad \deg x_i=2,$$
with $S_0=\mathbb R$ and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces $S_d$; the
symmetric group $S_n$ acts by the place permutations
$w\cdot x_i:=x_{w(i)}$ ([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]).
On this page $\alpha_i$ always means the coordinate root
$\alpha_i:=\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$, and $\alpha_i^\vee:=\beta_i^\vee$ is the
coordinate coroot, so that under the standard form the Cartan entries are
$\langle\alpha_i^\vee,\alpha_j\rangle=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{|i-j|,1}$ and
adjacent entries are $-1$; the reflection is
$s_i(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha_i\rangle\alpha_i^\vee$. The alternating balanced
roots $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}$ are retained by the published page for its
diagrammatic presentation and are not used for positivity, Demazure traces or
descent signs on this page; both choices define the same reflections, the same
reflecting hyperplanes, the same invariant rings $S^{s_i}$ and the same
underlying bimodules, and they differ only by the unit $\pm1$ in front of the
root, which changes no tensor bimodule but does change the normalization of
$\partial_i$ and of the trace.

**The real generators and the real category.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ set
$$B_i^R:=S\otimes_{S^{s_i}}S(1),$$
the balanced tensor product of the $(S,S^{s_i})$-bimodule $S$ with the
$(S^{s_i},S)$-bimodule $S$, shifted in the Elias-Williamson convention
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$ used on this page ([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]],
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Its left basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ have degrees $-1$ and $+1$, and
$B_i^R$ is finite free of rank two on each side
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]). The **real
type-A Soergel category** $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ is the idempotent completion
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) of the full subcategory of graded
$(S,S)$-bimodules whose objects are the finite direct sums of shifts
$B_{\underline i}^R(d)=B_{i_1}^R\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{i_r}^R(d)$ of real
Bott-Samelson products ([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with the
same internal shifts as the rational category, i.e. $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$ in the
Elias-Williamson convention. Its unit is the graded ring $S$ itself, regarded
as an object in cohomological degree zero; it is not a polynomial ring
concentrated in internal degree zero. Categorically,
$\mathrm{SBim}_n^R=\mathrm{Kar}(\mathrm{BSBim}_n^R)$ has the same formal
properties as the rational Soergel category: it is graded, additive,
idempotent-complete and monoidal with unit $S$, and every object is a finite
direct sum of graded shifts of indecomposables.

**Scalar extension of objects.** For a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ over the
rational polynomial ring put $M^R:=M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, with the
$S$-actions induced from the $R$-actions and the tensor grading. Since
$\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R$ is flat, scalar extension is exact on graded pieces;
it carries the rational generator $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ to $B_i^R$, the
rational Bott-Samelson construction to the real one, and the rational
idempotent completion to the real one. Standard graph supports, the
$\Delta$- and $\nabla$-flags with their characters, and all formulas of the
rational page are read over $\mathbb R$ after extension. The Hecke algebra
used for characters is the integral normalized algebra
$H_v(n)$ over $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with basis $H_x$ of
[[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]; it is the same
algebra before and after the scalar extension, since it is defined over
$\mathbb Z$.

**The dominant chamber.** The **dominant chamber** on this page is the set of
strictly dominant degree-two elements
$$\Theta:=\Bigl\{\rho=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j\ :\ c_j\in\mathbb R,\ c_j>c_{j+1}\ \text{for } 1\le j\le n-1\Bigr\}\subset S_2 .$$
It is nonempty, for example for $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$, which gives
$c_j-c_{j+1}=1$ for every $j$. For $\rho=\sum_jc_jx_j$ the coordinate
evaluation is $\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)=\rho(x_i-x_{i+1})=c_i-c_{i+1}$, so
$\rho\in\Theta$ is exactly a degree-two element with
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot; no alternating-sign chamber
and no replacement of $\rho$ is used anywhere on this page.

**Conventions.** All tensor products are over $S$ unless indicated, all shifts
are the internal shifts just fixed, "form" on this page always means a graded
symmetric form that is $S$-bilinear for the right action and invariant under
the left action in the sense fixed by the intersection-form definition below, and
dimensions of reduced modules are always real dimensions. The rational
comparison statements needed for labels, characters and forms are collected
in the comparison lemma later on this page.

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$, both of degrees $-1$ and $1$; and every
Bott–Samelson tensor product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite
free as a left $R$-module and finite free as a right $R$-module.

derivations.claim: The unit has the perfect multiplication form. If a right-free bimodule $M$ has an invariant form, put $a(b)=b c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $b(b')=b'c_s$ in $MB_s$ and define the induced form by $\langle a(u),a(v)\rangle=\partial_s\langle u,v\rangle$, $\langle a(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle b(u),a(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle$, and $\langle b(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle\alpha_s$. Extend on a right basis by right bilinearity. The relation of [F2] and the identity $\partial_s(fr)=\partial_s(f)r+s(f)\partial_s(r)$ verify that these formulas agree for arbitrary $u,v$, and that left multiplication is self-adjoint. Symmetry follows from symmetry of the preceding form. If $e_i,e_i^*$ are dual right bases for that form, the pairing between bases $(a(e_i),b(e_i))$ and $(b(e_i^*),a(e_i^*))$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\\alpha_sI&I\end{pmatrix}$, using $\partial_s(1)=0$, and has determinant one. Thus perfection is preserved. Iteration yields a perfect symmetric invariant form on every word, exactly its successive rank-one trace multiplication form.

For finite right-free modules the graded double-dual evaluation is an isomorphism, so $D$ is an involutive contravariant equivalence and takes indecomposables to indecomposables. The invariant perfect word form of step 1.1 identifies a word with its right dual. Generic graph support is unchanged by this duality: in a right basis left multiplication matrices transpose under $D$, so their simultaneous eigencharacters, and hence the graph labels after passing to the polynomial fraction field, are unchanged. A right-free summand has precisely the support closure of those graph labels. Therefore $DB_x$ is an indecomposable summand with the $x$ graph of the same reduced word. Uniqueness in [F1] identifies it with $B_x$ with no shift.

A word of length $m$ has a homogeneous right basis given by tensor products of the two basis elements in [F2]; its generator degrees lie between $-m$ and $m$ and have parity $m$. Right reduction preserves a split direct-sum decomposition. Since $B_x$ is an unshifted summand of its reduced word of length $m=\ell(x)$, its reduction has these same bounds and parity. The word's bottom degree is the single $1$-tensor. The balanced evaluation of that word on its top graph, obtained by successively twisting the tensor-slot polynomials by the successive prefix permutations, sends this $1$-tensor to $1$. It factors through the rank-one top quotient, and is an isomorphism onto $R_x(m)$ because both generators have degree $-m$. All other summands have no $x$ support; consequently the projection of the bottom tensor into $B_x$ is nonzero. Its bottom dimension is therefore one.

Right duality reverses the degrees of the finite homogeneous basis after reduction. The unshifted duality $DB_x\cong B_x$ from step 2.1 therefore makes the reduced dimensions symmetric and gives top dimension one from the bottom dimension in step 3.1. The perfect trace forms, duality, degree bounds, parity and extremal dimensions have now all been established locally.
